intro: Who is Israel in the promises of God? The Old Testament promised Abraham a seed, a land and blessing for the nations (Genesis 12:1-3). It promised David a son on an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12-16), and it promised Jerusalem a glorious temple, a return from exile and a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Christians agree that these promises meet in Jesus Christ, 'the Son of David, the son of Abraham' (Matthew 1:1). They disagree about what that means for the Jewish people and for the land. The fulfilment family (covenant amillennialists, postmillennialists, partial preterists and progressive covenantalists) holds that every promise has found its 'Yes' in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20) and now belongs to all who are in him, Jew and Gentile alike, so that no second, national fulfilment is required. The future family (historic premillennialists in part, progressive and classic dispensationalists, and Christian Zionists) holds that God will still keep his specific promises to ethnic, national Israel, including the land and a kingdom centred on Jerusalem, because 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable' (Romans 11:29). This study traces each promise from its first giving to where the New Testament says it lands. It sets out the history of the modern State of Israel, founded in 1948, and asks whether that state fulfils prophecy. It weighs the present reign of Christ against a future earthly kingdom. Each camp is given in its strongest form, with its best answers. The theological question is kept separate from the dignity of the Jewish people, whom both families are bound to love (Romans 10:1).

stakes.title: Who are the people of God?
stakes.text: If believing Gentiles are 'Abraham's seed, heirs according to the promise' (Galatians 3:29), then the church is the one continuing people of God, rooted in Israel's olive tree (Romans 11:17). If Israel and the church are two peoples with two sets of promises, then the church is a distinct new body, and national Israel still waits for its own inheritance. The answer shapes how believers read their own place in the story of Scripture.

stakes.title: How the two Testaments fit together
stakes.text: The debate is at bottom a debate about method. Does the New Testament explain the true sense of Old Testament promises (Luke 24:27, 44-45), or must every promise be kept in the exact form in which Israel first heard it? Each answer produces a different reading of the prophets, of Revelation 20 and of Romans 11. Readers who settle this question usually settle the rest.

stakes.title: Is Christ reigning now on David's throne?
stakes.text: Peter preached that God raised Jesus to sit on David's throne (Acts 2:30-36). Fulfilment scholars take this to mean the Davidic kingdom is already present, from heaven, and spreads by the gospel. Dispensationalists traditionally place the Davidic reign in a future millennium in Jerusalem; progressive dispensationalists say it has begun now and will be completed on earth later. The question decides whether Christians wait for the kingdom or live already within it.

stakes.title: Prophecy, politics and the Middle East
stakes.text: Since 1948, and especially since the Six-Day War in 1967, many Christians have read the modern State of Israel as fulfilled prophecy and have given it strong political support on that basis (Genesis 12:3). Others, including many Palestinian and Arab Christians, argue that this reading turns a political state into a sacred object and overlooks justice for all peoples in the land. The study separates what Scripture teaches from what any government does, and takes no side on current political or military disputes.

stakes.title: Love for the Jewish people
stakes.text: Paul grieved for his kinsmen and prayed for their salvation (Romans 9:1-5; Romans 10:1). He warned Gentile believers not to boast against the natural branches (Romans 11:18-21) and said that the Jewish people remain 'beloved for the sake of their forefathers' (Romans 11:28). The long history of Christian contempt for Jews, from medieval expulsions to the Holocaust, demands care in this debate. Neither family, at its best, teaches hatred; the question is how God's love for Israel is expressed in Christ.

camps.name: Covenant amillennialism
camps.summary: Covenant amillennialists read the Bible as one unfolding covenant of grace, from the promise in Genesis 3:15 to the new creation. The promises made to Abraham, Moses and David are not cancelled but fulfilled in Christ, the true Israel, and shared by all who are united to him by faith. The 'thousand years' of Revelation 20 is the present age between Christ's first and second comings, in which Christ reigns and Satan is bound so that the gospel reaches the nations. The hope of the believer is not a restored Jewish kingdom but the new heavens and new earth.
camps.israel: Israel was always defined by promise and faith, not by birth alone: 'not all who are descended from Israel are Israel' (Romans 9:6). Jesus, the obedient Son, embodies Israel (Matthew 2:15), and all who belong to him, believing Jews and Gentiles together, form 'the Israel of God' (Galatians 6:16). The church is not a replacement of Israel but Israel's faithful remnant enlarged by the grafting in of Gentiles (Romans 11:17-24).
camps.land: The land of Canaan was a real gift and a type. Abraham himself looked for a heavenly country and a city with foundations (Hebrews 11:10, 16), and Paul says the promise was that he would inherit 'the world' (Romans 4:13). The land promise widens in Christ to the whole renewed earth, which the meek will inherit (Matthew 5:5).
camps.kingdom: The kingdom of God came with Christ, is present now as he reigns from heaven at the right hand of God (Ephesians 1:20-22), and will be revealed in fullness at his single return. There is no future earthly millennium; the next great event is the return of Christ, the general resurrection and the judgment.
camps.modernState: The modern state is not seen as a fulfilment of prophecy. It is a political entity, founded by a largely secular Zionist movement in 1948 and judged like any other nation. Its people are loved and evangelised like all others, and many amillennialists take care to reject antisemitism.
camps.romans11: Views differ. Calvin read 'all Israel' as the whole church of Jews and Gentiles. Bavinck, Hoekema, Robertson and Hendriksen read it as the full number of elect Jews saved through the whole age. Some amillennialists, such as Kim Riddlebarger, expect a future large-scale turning of Jews to Christ before his return, without any national kingdom.
scholars: Augustine of Hippo (The City of God, c. 426)
Anthony Hoekema (The Bible and the Future, 1979)
O. Palmer Robertson (The Israel of God, 2000)
Cornelis Venema (The Promise of the Future, 2000)

camps.name: Postmillennialism
camps.summary: Postmillennialists share covenant theology's reading of the promises but are optimistic about history. Christ reigns now from heaven, and through the preaching of the gospel and the work of the Spirit most of the world's peoples will be converted before he returns (Psalms 2:8; Matthew 28:18-20). The millennium is the long era of gospel triumph that comes before the second coming. Many postmillennialists, following the Puritans, expect the conversion of the Jewish people to be part of that triumph.
camps.israel: The church of Jew and Gentile is the one people of God and the heir of Israel's promises. Yet ethnic Jews keep a special place in God's providence: their future conversion will bring 'life from the dead' for the world (Romans 11:15). This is a conversion into the one church, not the creation of a separate national people.
camps.land: The land promise is fulfilled in Christ and extends to the whole earth, which will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord as the waters cover the sea (Isaiah 11:9; Habakkuk 2:14). Some older postmillennialists, such as some Puritans, did expect Jews to return to Palestine, but this was not central to the system.
camps.kingdom: Christ's Davidic kingdom is already reigning and will grow like a mustard seed until it fills the earth (Matthew 13:31-33). There is no future earthly kingdom after Christ returns; his return closes history with resurrection and judgment.
camps.modernState: Most modern postmillennialists see the State of Israel as a secular political state with no prophetic standing. They hope for Jewish people to come to Christ, not for the state's expansion. Some note that earlier Puritan hopes were for the conversion of the Jews, not for a state founded without faith in Christ.
camps.romans11: Most expect a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews within the church, leading to wider blessing for the nations. This is the 'Puritan hope' traced by Iain Murray. A minority read 'all Israel' as the whole elect church.
scholars: Jonathan Edwards (A History of the Work of Redemption, 1739 sermons)
Kenneth L. Gentry Jr. (He Shall Have Dominion, 1992)

camps.name: Partial preterism
camps.summary: Partial preterists hold that many prophecies which others place in the future were fulfilled in the first century, above all in the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by Rome in AD 70 (Matthew 24:34). Jesus warned that the kingdom would be taken from the leaders of Israel and given to a people producing its fruit (Matthew 21:43), and that judgment would fall on 'this generation' (Matthew 23:36). AD 70 marked the end of the old covenant order and showed that the new covenant people in Christ is God's temple. Partial preterists still hold to Christ's future bodily return, the resurrection and the final judgment, which separates them from full preterism, a view outside the historic creeds.
camps.israel: The true Israel is the Messiah and the remnant who believed in him, joined by the Gentiles. Old covenant Israel as a national, temple-centred institution came to its appointed end in AD 70. Ethnic Jews remain loved and are called to the same faith as all others.
camps.land: The land, temple and Jerusalem served their purpose as shadows until the coming of Christ (Hebrews 8:13). The heavenly Jerusalem is now 'our mother' (Galatians 4:26), and believers have come to Mount Zion (Hebrews 12:22).
camps.kingdom: The kingdom came with power in the generation of the apostles (Mark 9:1) and is now advancing. Most partial preterists are postmillennial, a few are amillennial. None expect a future earthly Jewish kingdom.
camps.modernState: The modern state has no prophetic link to texts that, on this view, were fulfilled by AD 70. Preterists criticise 'newspaper exegesis' and the many failed predictions tied to 1948 and 1967. Some debate whether 'until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled' (Luke 21:24) hints at a later change for Jerusalem; this is disputed among them.
camps.romans11: Opinions vary. Many partial preterists, following the Puritans, expect a future conversion of Jews to Christ; others read 'all Israel' as the whole people of God.
scholars: Kenneth L. Gentry Jr. (Before Jerusalem Fell, 1989)
R. C. Sproul (The Last Days According to Jesus, 1998)
Keith A. Mathison (When Shall These Things Be?, 2004)

camps.name: Progressive covenantalism
camps.summary: Progressive covenantalism, set out by Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum in Kingdom through Covenant (2012), reads the Bible as a series of covenants (Noah, Abraham, Israel, David) that progressively unfold and are all fulfilled in the new covenant in Christ. It agrees with dispensationalists that the new covenant is truly new, and with covenant theologians that Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ. The key move is typology: Israel, the land and the temple are real historical types whose antitype is Christ and, through him, his people.
camps.israel: Christ is the true Israel, the obedient Son and Servant (Isaiah 49:3). The church is not simply 'the new Israel' by direct transfer, but it receives Israel's promises because it is united to Christ, Israel's antitype. Ethnic Jews who believe are part of this one new man (Ephesians 2:15).
camps.land: The land is a type of the new creation. Oren Martin in Bound for the Promised Land (2015) traces how the land promise, already pointing back to Eden, widens to the whole renewed world (Romans 4:13; Revelation 21:1-3). A restoration of Canaan alone would be a step back from the fulfilment.
camps.kingdom: The kingdom was inaugurated by Christ's death, resurrection and enthronement and will be consummated at his return. Most progressive covenantalists are amillennial, though some are historic premillennial; the system does not require one view of Revelation 20.
camps.modernState: The 1948 state is not regarded as a fulfilment of prophecy, since the promises run through Christ, not apart from him. Proponents usually stress love and evangelism toward Jewish people.
camps.romans11: Thomas Schreiner and others hold that Romans 11:26 promises a future large-scale salvation of ethnic Jews through faith in Christ. This conversion does not bring a separate national kingdom.
scholars: Oren R. Martin (Bound for the Promised Land, 2015)

camps.name: Historic premillennialism
camps.summary: Historic premillennialists, following early writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, expect Christ to return before an earthly reign of a thousand years (Revelation 20:4-6). Unlike dispensationalists, most do not hold a strict distinction between Israel and the church, and they agree that the church shares in Israel's promises now. George Eldon Ladd argued that the New Testament reinterprets Old Testament prophecy around Christ. Yet many in this camp still expect a future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ, linked to his return.
camps.israel: The church is the people of God and the spiritual Israel, but ethnic Israel has not lost its place in God's purposes. Ladd held that 'all Israel' in Romans 11:26 means a future salvation of literal Israel, within the one people of God. Some, like Barry Horner, argue strongly for a continuing national identity.
camps.land: Views vary. Ladd tended to read the land promises through Christ. Others in this camp, such as Barry Horner and earlier writers like J. C. Ryle and C. H. Spurgeon, expected the Jews to be restored to their land.
camps.kingdom: The kingdom is 'already and not yet': it came in Christ's ministry and is present in power (Matthew 12:28), but it will appear on earth in an intermediate millennial reign after Christ returns, before the eternal state.
camps.modernState: Views vary widely. Some see the modern state as a providential event that may prepare for Israel's future turning to Christ; others, like Ladd, refused to tie prophecy to any political state.
camps.romans11: Most expect a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews at or just before Christ's return (Romans 11:25-27; Zechariah 12:10). This conversion opens the millennial blessing.
scholars: George Eldon Ladd (The Presence of the Future, 1974)

camps.name: Progressive dispensationalism
camps.summary: Progressive dispensationalism arose in the 1980s and 1990s through Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock and Robert Saucy. It agrees that Christ already reigns on David's throne from heaven (Acts 2:30-36) and that the church shares in the new covenant now. But it insists that the kingdom will be completed on earth, with a restored and saved national Israel in its land among the redeemed nations. Its model is 'already and not yet': the Davidic promises are inaugurated now and consummated in the millennium and new creation.
camps.israel: Israel means ethnic, national Israel, and the church is a multi-ethnic people that includes Jews and Gentiles. Gentiles share in Israel's spiritual blessings without becoming Israel, just as the nations in the prophets are blessed alongside Israel (Isaiah 19:24-25). Michael Vlach stresses that nations remain nations in the new creation (Revelation 21:24-26).
camps.land: The land promise to Abraham's physical descendants remains in force (Genesis 17:8). It will be fulfilled when Christ returns and Israel, saved and restored, lives securely in its land within a renewed earth that also includes the nations.
camps.kingdom: Jesus now reigns on David's throne in heaven, but the kingdom will come on earth in a future millennium, with Jerusalem as a centre, followed by the eternal state. The apostles' question about restoring the kingdom to Israel was about timing, not about whether it would happen (Acts 1:6-7).
camps.modernState: Most progressive dispensationalists are cautious. They distinguish the secular state from the future restoration of Israel in faith (Ezekiel 36:24-28), while allowing that God may be preparing the way. They urge justice for all peoples in the land.
camps.romans11: Romans 11:26 promises a future national salvation of ethnic Israel when the Deliverer comes from Zion (Romans 11:26-27). This salvation leads to national restoration in the land.
scholars: Robert L. Saucy (The Case for Progressive Dispensationalism, 1993)
Michael J. Vlach (Has the Church Replaced Israel?, 2010)

camps.name: Classic dispensationalism
camps.summary: Classic dispensationalism, shaped by John Nelson Darby in the 1830s and spread by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), reads history as a series of dispensations. It holds that God has two distinct peoples: Israel, with earthly promises, and the church, with heavenly ones. The church age is a 'parenthesis' or 'intercalation' not seen by the Old Testament prophets. After the rapture of the church, God will resume his program with Israel in the seventieth week of Daniel (Daniel 9:24-27) and then fulfil the land and throne promises literally in a thousand-year kingdom.
camps.israel: Israel always means the physical descendants of Jacob. Charles Ryrie named a consistent distinction between Israel and the church as the essential mark of dispensationalism, alongside literal interpretation and the glory of God as the unifying theme. Galatians 6:16 refers to believing Jews, not to the whole church.
camps.land: The land grant from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates (Genesis 15:18-21) is unconditional and eternal (Genesis 17:8). Israel has never possessed all of it permanently, so it awaits a literal fulfilment in the millennium (Amos 9:14-15).
camps.kingdom: The Davidic kingdom was offered to Israel by Jesus, rejected, and postponed. It will be set up on earth when Christ returns, with Christ ruling from Jerusalem over a restored Israel and the nations, and with a rebuilt millennial temple (Ezekiel 40-48).
camps.modernState: Most classic dispensationalists see the 1948 return as a significant step in God's prophetic program, often linked to a regathering in unbelief that comes before spiritual renewal (Ezekiel 37:7-10). Leading writers such as John Walvoord treated it as a sign of the approaching end, though careful scholars avoid setting dates.
camps.romans11: Romans 11:26 means a future national salvation of ethnic Israel at the second coming, after the tribulation, when the nation looks on the one they pierced (Zechariah 12:10).

camps.name: Christian Zionism
camps.summary: Christian Zionism is a theological and political movement, not one academic school. It holds that God's covenant with Abraham gives the Jewish people a continuing right to the land, and that Christians should support the return of Jews to it and, today, the State of Israel. Its roots lie in English Puritan and evangelical hopes, in figures such as Lord Shaftesbury and William Hechler (an ally of Theodor Herzl), and in William Blackstone's 1891 memorial to the U.S. president. Since 1967 it has grown into a large movement, with organisations such as Christians United for Israel (founded 2006).
camps.israel: Israel means the Jewish people as an ethnic and national people. Many Christian Zionists are dispensational, but some, such as Gerald McDermott's 'new Christian Zionism' (2016), argue from Scripture and church history without a full dispensational system.
camps.land: The land promise is permanent and still belongs to the Jewish people by divine gift (Genesis 17:8; Psalms 105:8-11). The return of Jews to the land in the twentieth century is seen as the hand of God.
camps.kingdom: Views on the kingdom differ, but most expect a future earthly kingdom centred on Jerusalem. Some focus less on end-time schemes and more on the present duty to bless Israel.
camps.modernState: The modern state is widely seen as a fulfilment, or at least a providential sign, of prophecies of return (Isaiah 66:8; Ezekiel 37:21-22). Supporting it is often read as obeying 'I will bless those who bless you' (Genesis 12:3). Critics, including many Palestinian Christians, say this confuses a modern political state with biblical Israel; proponents answer that God's faithfulness to the Jewish people includes the land.
camps.romans11: Romans 11:26 means a future salvation of the Jewish nation. Romans 11:28-29 is used to show that God's election of the Jewish people still stands, even in unbelief.
scholars: Hal Lindsey (The Late Great Planet Earth, 1970)
Gerald R. McDermott (ed., The New Christian Zionism, 2016)

branches.label: Christ the true Israel
branches.text: The fulfilment reading starts here: Jesus sums up Israel in himself. He is the Son, the Servant and the Vine, and the promises reach others only through him. Future-for-Israel scholars accept much of this typology but deny that it removes a future for the nation.

children.label: Called out of Egypt
children.text: Matthew applies Hosea's words about the nation to the child Jesus, so that Israel's story becomes his story.

children.label: The Servant named Israel
children.text: The Servant is called 'Israel', yet he also restores Israel and is a light to the nations (Isaiah 49:5-6).

children.label: The true vine
children.text: Israel was God's vine that gave bad fruit (Isaiah 5:7); Jesus calls himself the true vine and his disciples the branches.

children.label: All promises are Yes in him
children.text: Paul says every promise of God finds its 'Yes' in Christ.

branches.label: The seed of Abraham
branches.text: God promised Abraham a seed through whom all nations would be blessed. Paul reads 'seed' as pointing to one person, Christ, and then to all who belong to Christ.

children.label: The promise to Abraham
children.text: Abraham's seed will possess the gate of his enemies, and in his seed all nations will be blessed.

children.label: Seed, singular
children.text: Paul notes that the promise says 'seed', not 'seeds', and identifies the seed as Christ.

children.label: Heirs in Christ
children.text: Those who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise.

children.label: Children of the promise
children.text: Not the children of the flesh but the children of the promise are counted as the seed.

branches.label: The land
branches.text: Canaan was promised to Abraham and given under Joshua. The New Testament widens the inheritance to the world and the new creation; the future camp holds that Canaan itself will still be given to national Israel.

children.label: Promised to Abraham
children.text: God promised the land of Canaan to Abraham and his seed as an everlasting possession.

children.label: Given under Joshua
children.text: The Lord gave Israel all the land he had sworn to their fathers.

children.label: Heir of the world
children.text: The promise to Abraham was that he would be heir of the world.

children.label: The meek inherit the earth
children.text: Jesus widens Psalms 37:11 from the land to the earth.

branches.label: The temple
branches.text: The tabernacle and temple were God's dwelling among Israel. In the New Testament, Christ's body and then his people are the temple; Revelation's new Jerusalem has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple.

children.label: His body the temple
children.text: Jesus spoke of the temple of his body, to be raised in three days.

children.label: The church a holy temple
children.text: Jews and Gentiles together are built into a holy temple in the Lord.

children.label: A copy and shadow
children.text: The earthly sanctuary was a copy and shadow of the heavenly one.

children.label: No temple in the city
children.text: The Lord God and the Lamb are the temple of the new Jerusalem.

branches.label: Jerusalem and Zion
branches.text: Zion was the city of David and of the temple. The prophets promised that the nations would stream to it. Hebrews and Galatians speak of a heavenly Jerusalem to which believers have already come.

children.label: Nations stream to Zion
children.text: In the last days the nations come to the mountain of the Lord to learn his ways.

children.label: You have come to Mount Zion
children.text: Believers have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.

children.label: Jerusalem above
children.text: The Jerusalem above is free and is the mother of believers.

children.label: The new Jerusalem
children.text: The holy city comes down out of heaven from God as a bride.

branches.label: The throne of David
branches.text: God promised David a son whose throne would last forever. The apostles preached that Jesus was raised and enthroned to fulfil this promise; dispensationalists traditionally place his reign on David's throne in a future earthly kingdom.

children.label: The covenant with David
children.text: God promised to raise up David's offspring and establish his throne forever.

children.label: Given the throne of David
children.text: Gabriel says God will give Jesus the throne of his father David, and his kingdom will have no end.

children.label: Raised to sit on the throne
children.text: Peter says David foresaw that God would raise the Christ to sit on his throne.

children.label: At the right hand
children.text: Peter cites Psalms 110:1: the risen Jesus is made Lord and Christ.

branches.label: The people of God (ekklesia)
branches.text: Israel was the 'assembly' of the Lord. The New Testament uses Israel's titles for the church of Jews and Gentiles; dispensationalists hold that the church shares these titles without becoming Israel.

children.label: A kingdom of priests
children.text: God called Israel his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.

children.label: Titles given to the church
children.text: Peter gives Israel's titles to scattered believers who were once 'not a people'.

children.label: One new man
children.text: Christ made Jew and Gentile into one new man, making peace.

children.label: One olive tree
children.text: Gentiles are grafted into the one olive tree among the natural branches.

branches.label: The new covenant
branches.text: Jeremiah promised a new covenant with the house of Israel and Judah. Jesus inaugurated it in his blood, and Hebrews applies it to the church. The future camp agrees the church shares in it now but expects a national fulfilment for Israel.

children.label: Promised to Israel and Judah
children.text: God promised a new covenant with the law written on the heart and sins forgiven.

children.label: The cup of the covenant
children.text: Jesus calls the cup the new covenant in his blood.

children.label: Applied to the church
children.text: Hebrews quotes Jeremiah at length and says the first covenant is now obsolete.

children.label: Ministers of a new covenant
children.text: Paul calls the apostles ministers of a new covenant of the Spirit.

recapitulation.israel: God called Israel his firstborn son and demanded that Pharaoh let his son go.
recapitulation.jesus: At his baptism the Father calls Jesus his beloved Son, the one in whom he is pleased.

recapitulation.israel: God called his son Israel out of Egypt in the exodus.
recapitulation.jesus: The child Jesus goes down into Egypt and returns, and Matthew says this fulfils Hosea's words.

recapitulation.israel: Israel passed through the sea on dry ground; Paul calls this a baptism into Moses (1 Corinthians 10:1-2).
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus passes through the waters of the Jordan in baptism and the Spirit descends on him.

recapitulation.israel: Israel was tested forty years in the wilderness to show what was in its heart, and often failed.
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus is tested forty days in the wilderness and answers each temptation with words from Deuteronomy (8:3; 6:16; 6:13), succeeding where Israel failed.

recapitulation.israel: Moses went up Mount Sinai and brought God's law down to the people.
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus goes up on a mountain and teaches the law with his own authority: 'but I say to you'.

recapitulation.israel: Israel was made up of twelve tribes descended from the sons of Jacob.
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus chooses twelve apostles, a sign of Israel reconstituted around himself (compare Matthew 19:28).

recapitulation.israel: Israel was the Lord's vineyard, planted with choice vines, but it produced wild grapes.
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus says he is the true vine and his Father is the gardener; fruit comes by abiding in him.

recapitulation.israel: God calls his Servant 'Israel, in whom I will be glorified', and gives him a mission to Israel and the nations.
recapitulation.jesus: Matthew applies the Servant song of Isaiah 42 to Jesus, the chosen one in whom God delights.

recapitulation.israel: The glory of the Lord filled Solomon's temple, God's dwelling among his people.
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus calls his body the temple, to be destroyed and raised in three days.

recapitulation.israel: God promised to set over his scattered flock one shepherd, his servant David.
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.

recapitulation.israel: God fed Israel with manna, bread from heaven, in the wilderness.
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus says he is the bread of life, the true bread come down from heaven.

recapitulation.israel: Water flowed from the struck rock to give Israel drink; Paul says 'the rock was Christ' (1 Corinthians 10:4).
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus cries out that whoever is thirsty should come to him and drink, and rivers of living water will flow.

recapitulation.israel: Moses lifted up a bronze serpent, and those bitten who looked to it lived.
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus says the Son of Man must be lifted up in the same way, so that all who believe may have eternal life.

recapitulation.israel: Israel was spared when God saw the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts.
recapitulation.jesus: Paul says Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed.

recapitulation.israel: Jacob, who became Israel, saw a ladder joining heaven and earth with angels going up and down.
recapitulation.jesus: Jesus says his disciples will see angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man; he is the meeting place of heaven and earth.

recapitulation.israel: Hosea pictures Israel, torn and struck down, being raised up on the third day; the prophets used death and resurrection for exile and return (Ezekiel 37:12).
recapitulation.jesus: Christ died for our sins and was raised on the third day 'according to the Scriptures', bearing Israel's exile and leading the true return.

promises.title: The call of Abraham: a great nation and a blessing for all families
promises.promise: God tells Abram to leave his country and go to a land God will show him. God promises to make him a great nation, to bless him, to make his name great, and to make him a blessing. God will bless those who bless him and curse the one who treats him with contempt, and in him all the families of the earth will be blessed. The promise has three strands from the start: a people, a land, and a blessing that reaches every nation.

path.text: The call joins a nation, a land and a worldwide blessing. The blessing for 'all the families of the earth' answers the scattering of the nations in Genesis 11.
At the descent into Egypt God repeats that he will make Jacob's family a great nation there. By Exodus 1:7 the family has multiplied and filled the land of Goshen.

Paul says Scripture 'preached the gospel beforehand' to Abraham when it said that all nations would be blessed in him. The blessing is justification by faith, given to the nations in Christ (Galatians 3:14).
Peter tells the people of Jerusalem that they are heirs of the covenant with Abraham. God raised his Servant and sent him to them first, to bless them by turning each one from wickedness.
Abraham is 'the father of us all', Jew and Gentile who share his faith. Paul reads Genesis 17:5, 'father of many nations', as fulfilled in a believing family drawn from every people.
John sees a multitude no one can count, from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne. This is the 'all families of the earth' of Genesis 12:3 at the end of the story.

promises.history: Genesis places Abram's call after his family moved from Ur of the Chaldeans to Harran (Genesis 11:31-12:4), when he was seventy-five years old. Most conservative scholars place the patriarchs in the early second millennium BC (Middle Bronze Age), though the dating is disputed and some critical scholars doubt the narratives are historical at all. K. A. Kitchen argues that details such as treaty forms, personal names and slave prices fit the early second millennium. The first certain mention of 'Israel' as a people in Canaan outside the Bible is the Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC). By the time of the New Testament, Jewish teaching saw Abraham as the father of the nation and the model proselyte, which is why Paul's claim about 'the children of Abraham' (Galatians 3:7) was so sharp.
promises.toUs: A Gentile believer is not a guest in someone else's family story. Paul says that those who are of faith are sons of Abraham and are blessed with him (Galatians 3:7-9). The promise that began with one man leaving his country now includes every believer from every nation, and the mission of the church is the way 'all families' are being reached.
promises.futurist: Dispensational writers such as Walvoord, Pentecost and Fruchtenbaum agree that the blessing of the nations flows through Christ. But they hold that the Abrahamic covenant has distinct strands, and that Gentiles share in the spiritual blessing strand without taking over the national strand. The 'great nation' remains the physical descendants of Abraham through Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 17:19-21; 28:13-14). Christian Zionists add that Genesis 12:3 ('I will bless those who bless you') still applies to the Jewish people and so shapes how nations should treat them today.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers such as O. Palmer Robertson and Gentry and Wellum answer that Paul does not divide the promise into separate national and spiritual parts. He says the promise was spoken to Abraham 'and to his seed', which is Christ (Galatians 3:16), and that all who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed and heirs (Galatians 3:29). The blessing-and-curse clause was spoken first to Abraham himself, then passed to Jacob (Genesis 27:29) and to Israel as God's people (Numbers 24:9); in the New Testament the people who carry that blessing are those united to the Messiah. They add that physical descent alone never made one a child of the promise (Romans 9:6-8).
promises.rejoinder: Vlach and Saucy reply that Galatians 3 is about how Gentiles are saved, not about the future of the nation. Gentiles become Abraham's children by faith without becoming Israel, just as Genesis 12:3 itself distinguishes Abraham's nation from 'all the families' who are blessed through it. Paul still says that the promises 'belong' to his kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:4) and that God's calling of them is irrevocable (Romans 11:28-29).

promises.title: The land given to Abraham's seed, from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates
promises.promise: After Lot leaves, God tells Abram to look in every direction: all the land he can see will be given to him and his seed forever (Genesis 13:14-17). In Genesis 15 God binds himself by covenant. He passes alone between the cut animals as a smoking fire pot and a burning torch, and promises the land 'from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates', the land of ten named peoples.

path.text: God promises Abram all the land he can see, to him and to his seed forever, and a seed as many as the dust of the earth. Abram is told to walk through the land, but he owns none of it in his lifetime.
God alone passes between the pieces, binding himself to the promise. The borders run from 'the river of Egypt' to the Euphrates.
Under Solomon, the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt bring tribute and serve him. The Genesis 15 borders are reached in the form of a ruled empire.
Paul says the promise to Abraham and his seed was that he would be 'heir of the world'. The promise of Canaan is read as a pledge of the whole earth.
Abraham lived in the promised land as a foreigner, in tents. He looked for a city with foundations whose builder is God, and the patriarchs desired 'a better country, that is, a heavenly one'.
The promise ends in a new heaven and a new earth, where God dwells with his people. The 'land' has widened to the renewed creation (Matthew 5:5).

promises.history: The covenant ritual of Genesis 15 matches ancient Near Eastern oath rites in which parties walked between halved animals, calling the same fate on themselves if they broke faith. Jeremiah 34:18-19 describes the same rite, and eighth-century BC Aramaic treaties from Sefire contain similar curse formulas. 'The river of Egypt' (Hebrew nahar) is read by some as the Nile's eastern branch and by others as the Wadi el-Arish, the 'brook of Egypt' of Numbers 34:5; this is disputed. The northern border at the Euphrates was reached only under David and Solomon (2 Samuel 8:3; 1 Kings 4:21, 24), and then as an area of vassal states rather than settled tribal land. The extent of the united monarchy is itself debated by archaeologists (the 'low chronology' of Israel Finkelstein against the views of Amihai Mazar and others).
promises.toUs: The promise shows that God's salvation is not only for souls but for a place: God means his people to live with him in a real, good earth. Believers today are heirs of that promise, but like Abraham they live as strangers and pilgrims, waiting for the renewed earth (1 Peter 1:4; 2 Peter 3:13). Jesus' word that the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5, echoing Psalms 37:11) is the same promise in its widest form.
promises.futurist: Classic dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Ryrie) argue that an unconditional covenant, ratified by God alone, guarantees the land to Abraham's physical descendants in the exact borders of Genesis 15:18. Since Israel has never held all of this land permanently as its own possession, they hold the promise awaits the millennial kingdom (Ezekiel 47:13-48:29). Progressive dispensationalists such as Blaising, Bock and Saucy agree that the land will finally widen to the whole earth, but insist the widening includes, rather than replaces, the particular land of Israel.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers answer that the Old Testament itself already widens the land. Psalms 2:8 gives the Messiah 'the ends of the earth' as his possession, and Psalms 72:8 sets his rule 'from sea to sea'. Robertson, Martin and Burge argue that Paul's 'heir of the world' (Romans 4:13) and Hebrews 11 show how the apostles understood the land: as a type of the renewed creation. The final inheritance is therefore larger than Canaan, not smaller, and it belongs to all who are in Christ. W. D. Davies notes that the New Testament almost never repeats the promise of Canaan as such, and instead attaches the holiness of place to the person of Jesus.
promises.rejoinder: Vlach replies that 'widening' can still include the original land: the whole earth includes Canaan, just as the nations are blessed without Israel ceasing to be a nation. Saucy points to the New Testament's own hopes centred on Jerusalem (Luke 21:24; Acts 1:6-7), and Kaiser notes that God tied the land to the word 'forever' (Genesis 13:15). They argue that the silence of the New Testament on the land is an argument from silence and does not cancel explicit Old Testament oaths.

promises.title: An everlasting covenant: God to Abraham's seed, and Canaan an everlasting possession
promises.promise: God confirms his covenant with Abraham and his seed after him as an everlasting covenant: he will be their God. He will give Abraham and his seed all the land of Canaan, where he is now a foreigner, as an everlasting possession. Circumcision is given as the sign of the covenant in the flesh (Genesis 17:10-14).

path.text: The covenant formula 'I will be their God' is joined to land 'for an everlasting possession'. Circumcision marks the covenant people.
At the exodus God recalls the covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He promises to take Israel as his people, be their God, and bring them into the land he swore to give.
Paul notes that the promises were spoken to Abraham and 'to his seed', singular, 'which is Christ'. Christ is the true heir of the everlasting covenant.
If you belong to Christ, you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise. Circumcision of the heart, not of the flesh, now marks the covenant people (Romans 2:28-29; Colossians 2:11).
A loud voice says that God's dwelling is with people and that he will be their God and they will be his people. The covenant formula of Genesis 17:7 reaches its final form.

promises.history: The word translated 'everlasting' (Hebrew 'olam) is used in the Law for other institutions that the New Testament treats as ended or transformed in Christ: circumcision as an 'everlasting covenant' in the flesh (Genesis 17:13), the Passover as a statute 'forever' (Exodus 12:14), and the Aaronic priesthood as an 'everlasting priesthood' (Exodus 40:15; Numbers 25:13). Israel lost the land twice for long periods: the north to Assyria in 722 BC and Judah to Babylon in 586 BC. After AD 135 (the Bar Kokhba revolt), Jews were barred from Jerusalem, renamed Aelia Capitolina by Hadrian. The question of what 'everlasting possession' means is therefore pressed by history as well as by exegesis.
promises.toUs: The heart of the covenant is not real estate but relationship: 'I will be your God'. Believers in Christ share that covenant fully and will see it completed when God lives with his people forever. The same God who kept the promise to Abraham will keep his word to every believer.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists argue that 'everlasting' must mean what it says. Ryrie and Walvoord hold that because the covenant is unconditional and everlasting, physical Israel must possess Canaan forever, and the millennium and the eternal state will see that. Fruchtenbaum adds that Paul's 'seed' argument in Galatians 3:16 concerns the line of salvation, while Genesis also uses 'seed' collectively for the nation (Genesis 17:8 itself), so both senses stand.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers such as Robertson, Waltke and Holwerda reply that 'olam often means 'for the whole age of this covenant' and is used of things (circumcision, the Aaronic priesthood) that Hebrews 7:12 and Galatians 5:2-6 treat as fulfilled. The 'everlasting possession' is not lost but transposed: Canaan was the type of the everlasting inheritance, which is the renewed earth. In this reading, the promise is kept more fully, not cancelled, because believers will possess the whole earth forever (Romans 4:13; Revelation 21:1-7).
promises.rejoinder: Dispensational and premillennial writers (Horner, Vlach) answer that if 'everlasting' can be stretched so far, the eternal life promised to believers could be stretched too. They argue the right comparison is with God's promises, not with Mosaic rites, and that Jeremiah 31:35-37 ties Israel's survival as a nation to the fixed order of sun and moon. They also note that Genesis 17:8 names a particular land, 'all the land of Canaan', which is hard to read as a symbol.

promises.title: A seed like the stars and the sand, possessing the gate of its enemies
promises.promise: After Abraham offers Isaac on Mount Moriah, God swears by himself that he will greatly bless Abraham and multiply his seed as the stars of heaven and the sand on the seashore. His seed will possess the gate of his enemies, and in his seed all the nations of the earth will be blessed, because Abraham obeyed God's voice.

path.text: God swears an oath by himself. The promise of countless offspring is joined to victory over enemies and blessing for all nations 'in your seed'.
In Solomon's day Judah and Israel are 'as many as the sand by the sea', eating, drinking and rejoicing. Deuteronomy 1:10 had already said Israel was as the stars of heaven in number.
The 'seed' in whom the nations are blessed is Christ. Isaac, the offered and returned son (Hebrews 11:17-19), foreshadows the Son who is offered and raised.
All who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed. The countless offspring of the promise now includes Gentile believers (Romans 4:16-18).
The final multitude from every nation that no one can number fulfils the 'stars' and 'sand' in their widest sense. Hebrews 6:13-18 treats this oath as the anchor of Christian hope.

promises.history: 2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies Mount Moriah, the place of Isaac's binding, with the hill where Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. Jewish tradition (the Aqedah) made Isaac's binding a central theme of atonement and faith. By the census figures of Numbers 1 and 26 and the summary of 1 Kings 4:20, the Old Testament itself records that the promise of number was fulfilled in national form by the united monarchy. Yet after 586 BC only a remnant returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:64 counts 42,360 in the assembly), so the prophets looked ahead to a greater multiplication (Isaiah 54:1-3).
promises.toUs: Hebrews 6:13-20 says God swore by himself to Abraham so that those who flee to him for refuge might have strong encouragement. Every believer, Jew or Gentile, is part of the fulfilment of this oath. The growth of the church among all nations is God keeping his word to Abraham.
promises.futurist: Dispensational writers accept that Christ is the singular seed and that believers are spiritual seed. But Fruchtenbaum and Walvoord distinguish three senses of 'seed': the natural seed (all physical descendants), the spiritual seed within Israel (believing Jews), and the spiritual Gentile seed. Gentiles share the blessing but are never called 'Israel' in their reading. The national promise of number and victory over enemies will be seen when Israel as a nation is restored and saved (Romans 11:26).
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers answer that Paul does not keep a separate national seed in Galatians 3. He moves from the many (Abraham's offspring) to the one (Christ) and back to the many (all in Christ), as N. T. Wright stresses in The Climax of the Covenant. The 'gate of enemies' is seen in Christ's victory over death and the powers (Colossians 2:15) and the church's advance against the gates of Hades (Matthew 16:18). Ethnic Israel is not excluded: believing Jews are the first members of this seed (Romans 11:1-5).
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists answer that recognising believing Gentiles as Abraham's seed does not require saying the nation has no future. Romans 11 speaks of Israel 'according to the flesh' after Christ came, as 'beloved for the sake of the fathers' (Romans 11:28). In their reading the threefold seed makes better sense of all the uses of the word than a single spiritual sense does.

promises.title: A treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation
promises.promise: At Sinai God tells Israel that if they obey his voice and keep his covenant, they will be his treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is his. They will be to him a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The promise has a condition ('if you obey') and a purpose: Israel is to stand between God and the nations as a priest stands between God and the people.

path.text: Israel is called to be God's treasured people, a priestly kingdom and holy nation, on the condition of keeping the covenant.
The covenant is ratified with blood sprinkled on the people. Israel's national life under the Law serves as the pattern of a holy people.
Jesus gives the cup as 'the new covenant in my blood'. The covenant people is now formed around the Messiah's own blood, not the blood of Sinai.
Peter gives the church Israel's titles: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession. He adds Hosea's words: once not a people, now God's people.
The Lamb has ransomed people from every tribe and nation and made them a kingdom and priests to God, and they will reign on the earth.

promises.history: Exodus 19:1 dates the arrival at Sinai to the third month after the exodus. The covenant has the shape of an ancient Near Eastern vassal treaty: the history of what the great king has done (Exodus 20:2), stipulations, and blessings and curses (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28); scholars such as George Mendenhall and K. A. Kitchen compared it with Hittite treaties of the late second millennium BC, though the closest parallel is disputed. The date of the exodus is also disputed (a fifteenth-century date from 1 Kings 6:1, or a thirteenth-century date). Israel's history in Kings and Chronicles is largely the story of failure to keep this covenant, ending in exile.
promises.toUs: Every believer is a priest: able to draw near to God through Christ and called to make God known to others (1 Peter 2:5, 9). The church does not have a priestly caste between God and the people; the whole people is priestly. The holiness once marked by food laws and the temple is now marked by lives that 'proclaim the excellencies' of God.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists note that Peter writes to 'exiles of the dispersion' (1 Peter 1:1), which some, such as Fruchtenbaum, take as mainly Jewish believers. More broadly, Saucy and Vlach argue that Peter applies Israel's titles to the church by analogy, without saying the church has become Israel. They point to Isaiah 61:6, where Israel will be called 'priests of the LORD' while the nations serve them, and to Zechariah 8:23, where people from the nations take hold of a Jew's robe; this, they say, describes a future national priestly role.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers (Robertson, Beale, Hoekema) answer that Peter's language is not loose analogy. He gathers Exodus 19:6, Isaiah 43:20-21 and Hosea 2:23 and applies them to a mixed church, many of whom were Gentiles 'formerly not a people' (1 Peter 2:10; compare 1:14, 18 and 4:3 on their pagan past). Jesus had warned that the kingdom would be taken from the leaders of Israel and given to 'a nation producing its fruits' (Matthew 21:43). Revelation 1:6 and 5:10 then apply the same Exodus title to the whole redeemed people.
promises.rejoinder: Future-camp writers reply that Matthew 21:43 is addressed to the chief priests and Pharisees (Matthew 21:45), so it transfers stewardship from Israel's leaders, not from the nation forever. Revelation 5:10 says the redeemed will reign 'on the earth', which premillennialists of all kinds read as pointing to an earthly kingdom after Christ returns.

promises.title: Not one word failed: the land given under Joshua and Solomon
promises.promise: The book of Joshua closes the conquest with a strong summary. The LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to give their fathers; they took possession of it and lived in it. He gave them rest on every side, and not one of all the good promises he had made to Israel failed; all came to pass. Joshua repeats this in his farewell (Joshua 23:14), Solomon in his temple prayer (1 Kings 8:56), and the Levites in Nehemiah's day (Nehemiah 9:7-8).

path.text: God promises the land of the Kenites, Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites and others to Abraham's seed.
Joshua records that God gave all the land, gave rest, and that not one good word failed. Joshua 23:14 repeats it.
After the exile the Levites confess that God made a covenant with Abraham to give the land of the Canaanites and others, 'and you have kept your promise, for you are righteous'.
Hebrews says that if Joshua had given the final rest, God would not have spoken later of another day. A Sabbath rest remains for God's people, entered through faith in Christ.
The patriarchs died without receiving the promises in full and desired a better, heavenly country. God has prepared a city for them.

promises.history: The conquest is dated either to the late fifteenth century BC (from 1 Kings 6:1) or to the thirteenth century; the date and the archaeology of sites such as Jericho, Ai and Hazor remain disputed. The same book that says 'not one word failed' also says that 'very much land' remained to be taken (Joshua 13:1), and Judges 1 lists cities the tribes did not drive out. Under David and Solomon (tenth century BC) the rule of Israel reached from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt (2 Samuel 8:3; 1 Kings 4:21; 2 Chronicles 9:26), and Solomon's feast gathered Israel 'from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt' (1 Kings 8:65). Nehemiah 9 was prayed after the return from Babylon (mid-fifth century BC), yet still says God had kept his land promise.
promises.toUs: This argument reminds believers that God has a record of keeping promises in history. If he kept the land promise to the letter of his own word, he will keep his greater promise of an eternal inheritance (1 Peter 1:3-5). The Christian's rest is not a piece of territory but rest in Christ now and in the new creation later.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Fruchtenbaum) answer that Joshua 21:43-45 describes God's faithfulness in giving what the conquest generation could receive, not the final and permanent possession. Joshua 13:1 and Judges 1 show the land was not fully taken, and Solomon ruled vassal kings rather than settling the land with Israel's tribes. Above all, the prophets kept promising the land after Joshua and after Solomon (Jeremiah 32:37-41; Ezekiel 36:24-28; Amos 9:14-15, 'they shall never again be uprooted'), which, they argue, would make no sense if the promise had already been fully discharged.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers such as Robertson, Burge and Gentry and Wellum answer that Joshua deliberately holds both truths together: God gave all he promised, yet Israel's continued possession depended on faithfulness (Joshua 23:12-16). God's side of the promise was kept; the losses that followed came from covenant breaking, as Deuteronomy 28 had warned. The later prophetic promises of return were fulfilled in the return from Babylon (Ezra 1:1-4; Nehemiah 9:36-37), and their language of permanent security points beyond Canaan, as Hebrews 4 and 11 say. The New Testament never restates the land promise in territorial terms.
promises.rejoinder: Future-camp writers reply that the post-exilic return did not match Amos 9:15 or Ezekiel 37:25 ('forever'), because Israel was uprooted again in AD 70 and AD 135. So, they argue, the prophetic land promises cannot have been fulfilled in 538 BC. Kaiser also notes that the Old Testament repeats the land promise many times as a gift of grace, and that a conditional enjoyment of the land does not make the gift itself conditional.

promises.title: Exile and return: possession of the land under covenant conditions
promises.promise: Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 warn that if Israel breaks the covenant, they will be scattered among the nations and the land will lie desolate. Yet Leviticus 26:40-45 and Deuteronomy 30:1-6 promise that when the people return to the LORD in exile, he will remember his covenant with the fathers, gather them from the nations, bring them back to the land, and circumcise their hearts so that they love him with all their heart.

path.text: If the exiles confess their sin, God will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, and will remember the land. He will not reject them utterly.
After curse and scattering, God will restore and gather Israel and bring them into the land, and he will circumcise their hearts.
In the first year of Cyrus, God stirs the king to let the Jews return and rebuild the house of the LORD in Jerusalem.
Caiaphas unknowingly prophesies that Jesus would die for the nation, and not only for the nation but to gather into one the scattered children of God.

Paul reads Deuteronomy 30:12-14 ('the word is near you') as the word of faith in Christ: confess Jesus as Lord and believe God raised him. The heart-circumcision of Deuteronomy 30:6 comes by the Spirit (Romans 2:28-29).
Paul speaks of the coming of the Lord Jesus and 'our being gathered together to him', the final ingathering of God's scattered people.

promises.history: The curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 were carried out in history. Assyria destroyed Samaria and deported the northern tribes in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5-23). Babylon took Jerusalem in 597 BC (recorded in the Babylonian Chronicle, which dates the capture to 2 Adar, 16 March 597 BC) and destroyed the city and temple in 586 BC (2 Kings 25). Ostraca from Lachish describe the last days before the fall. Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, and his decree (Ezra 1:1-4; 6:3-5) allowed a return in 538 BC; the Cyrus Cylinder, found at Babylon in 1879, records his general policy of restoring displaced peoples and their sanctuaries. 2 Chronicles 36:20-23 links the exile to Jeremiah's seventy years and to the land enjoying its Sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34-35).
promises.toUs: The pattern of exile and return teaches that God disciplines his people but does not abandon them. The greatest 'return' is a return of the heart, which God himself works by the Spirit through the gospel. Believers live as people already gathered to Christ, waiting for the final gathering at his coming.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists argue that Deuteronomy 30 describes a final regathering that is followed by national heart-circumcision, and that the return of 538 BC did not meet that standard: most Jews stayed in the dispersion, the returnees remained under foreign rule (Nehemiah 9:36-37), and no national heart-change took place. Ezekiel 36:24-28 puts the regathering before the giving of the new heart. Many dispensationalists, following Walvoord and Fruchtenbaum, therefore see the regathering since the late nineteenth century, and the State of Israel founded in 1948, as at least the beginning of a regathering in unbelief, like the bones gathering before the breath comes in Ezekiel 37:7-10.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers answer that the Old Testament itself presents the return under Cyrus as the fulfilment of these promises (Ezra 1:1; 2 Chronicles 36:22; Daniel 9:2), and that the 'new heart' promise is applied by the New Testament to the gift of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:33; 2 Corinthians 3:3-6). Paul reads Deuteronomy 30 itself as speaking of Christ (Romans 10:6-9). Robertson and Burge argue that the 1948 state, founded by a largely secular movement, cannot be the return of Deuteronomy 30, since that return is defined as a return to the LORD 'with all your heart and soul' (Deuteronomy 30:2). The prophetic order is repentance, then return.
promises.rejoinder: Future-camp writers reply that Ezekiel 36-37 clearly has a regathering before spiritual renewal, so a return in unbelief is not ruled out. They also note that Deuteronomy 30:3-5 speaks of gathering from 'all the peoples' and from 'the ends of heaven', which the small return from Babylon and Persia does not match. Progressive dispensationalists are more cautious about 1948 but still expect a future national turning and restoration.

promises.title: The Davidic covenant: a son on David's throne forever
promises.promise: Through Nathan, God promises David that after his death he will raise up David's offspring and establish his kingdom. This son will build a house for God's name, and God will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. God will be his father and he will be God's son; if he does wrong God will discipline him, but God's steadfast love will not depart from him. David's house and kingdom will be made sure forever, and his throne established forever. Psalms 89:3-4 and Psalms 132:11-12 call this promise a sworn oath.

path.text: God promises David an offspring who will build God's house and whose throne will last forever. He will be God's son.
Solomon says God has kept his word: he has risen in David's place, sits on the throne of Israel, and has built the house for the LORD's name.
God has sworn to David that he will establish his offspring forever and build his throne for all generations. Psalms 89:38-51 then laments that the crown has been cast to the ground.
Gabriel says God will give Jesus the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever; of his kingdom there will be no end.

Peter says David knew God had sworn with an oath to seat one of his descendants on his throne, and foresaw the resurrection of the Christ. Jesus, raised and exalted to God's right hand, has been made Lord and Christ.
The kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he will reign forever and ever.

promises.history: The Tel Dan Stele, found in fragments in 1993 and 1994 at Tel Dan in northern Israel, is an Aramaic inscription of the ninth century BC, probably set up by Hazael of Damascus. It boasts of victory over a king of Israel and a king of 'the house of David' (bytdwd), the earliest known reference outside the Bible to David's dynasty. Davidic kings ruled in Jerusalem for about four centuries until Zedekiah was blinded and taken to Babylon in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:7). Jehoiachin was released in exile (2 Kings 25:27-30), and Babylonian ration tablets name 'Yaukin, king of the land of Yahud'. After the exile, Zerubbabel of David's line was governor but not king (Haggai 1:1), and the Hasmonean rulers (from 142 BC) and Herod were not Davidic. By the first century, Jewish hope looked for a 'son of David' (Psalms of Solomon 17, first century BC), and the Qumran text 4Q174 reads 2 Samuel 7 as a promise of the 'Branch of David'.
promises.toUs: The King believers serve is not a rival to David's line but its promised heir. Jesus reigns now as the risen Son of David at God's right hand, and every believer lives under that reign. Hebrews 1:5 applies 2 Samuel 7:14 ('I will be his father') to Christ, and 2 Corinthians 6:18 extends the father-son language to all believers.
promises.futurist: Classic dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Ryrie) hold that Christ now sits on his Father's throne in heaven (Revelation 3:21), but that 'the throne of David' is an earthly throne in Jerusalem which he will take at his return (Matthew 25:31; Luke 1:32-33). Luke 1:33 speaks of reigning over 'the house of Jacob', which they read as national Israel. Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock, Saucy) go further: they agree that Acts 2 shows the Davidic reign has been inaugurated at the ascension, but say its earthly, national phase will be completed in the millennium. Both forms cite Acts 1:6-7, where Jesus does not deny that the kingdom will be restored to Israel.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers (Riddlebarger, Hoekema, Robertson, Gentry and Wellum) answer that Peter explicitly links the oath to David with the resurrection and ascension: God swore to seat David's descendant on his throne, and David 'foresaw and spoke of the resurrection' (Acts 2:30-31). The throne at God's right hand is therefore the throne of David in its final form. Revelation 3:21 speaks of one shared throne, and Revelation 22:1 calls it 'the throne of God and of the Lamb'. Augustine (City of God 17) already read the promise of an eternal house as fulfilled in Christ and his church, since the Solomonic line failed.
promises.rejoinder: Progressive dispensationalists reply that 'inaugurated' does not mean 'exhausted'. Bock argues that Acts 3:19-21 still speaks of 'times of restoration' that come when Jesus returns, and that Luke-Acts keeps Israel's national hope alive. Classic dispensationalists add that the Old Testament places the Davidic throne in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 33:17; Isaiah 9:7), and that Christ sitting at the right hand is a temporary waiting 'until' (Psalms 110:1).

promises.title: The king set on Zion and seated at God's right hand
promises.promise: Psalms 2 says God has set his king on Zion, his holy hill. The king is God's son, and God will give him the nations as his inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession. Psalms 110 has the LORD say to David's Lord: sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool. The LORD will send out his mighty rod from Zion, and he will rule in the midst of his enemies. God has sworn: you are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.

path.text: God sets his king on Zion, calls him 'my Son', and promises him the nations and the ends of the earth.
Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, blesses Abram. He joins king and priest in one person, the pattern Psalms 110:4 takes up.
Paul says God has fulfilled the promise to the fathers by raising Jesus, as Psalms 2 says: 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you.'
Peter quotes Psalms 110:1. David did not ascend to heaven; Jesus did, and God has made him Lord and Christ.
God raised Christ and seated him at his right hand far above every rule and authority, put all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the church.
Christ must reign until God has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy destroyed is death; then comes the end, when he hands the kingdom to the Father.

promises.history: Psalms 2 and 110 were probably royal psalms used at the enthronement of Davidic kings in Jerusalem; Psalms 110 is attributed to David in its heading. Psalms 110:1 is the Old Testament text most often quoted or echoed in the New Testament. Jesus used it to ask how David's son could be David's Lord (Matthew 22:41-46). Before Christianity, Jewish writers already read Psalms 2 of the coming Messiah: Psalms of Solomon 17 uses the 'rod of iron' image, and the Qumran Florilegium (4Q174) links Psalms 2 with 2 Samuel 7. Melchizedek is also a heavenly figure in the Qumran text 11Q13 (11QMelchizedek).
promises.toUs: The reign of Christ is not only a future hope; he is seated and ruling now. The church's mission goes out from the risen King, who has 'all authority in heaven and on earth' (Matthew 28:18). Because he is also priest forever, believers have a permanent high priest who intercedes for them (Hebrews 7:23-25).
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists stress the word 'until' in Psalms 110:1. Christ now sits at the Father's right hand and waits; the active rule 'from Zion' over enemies (Psalms 110:2) and the striking of the nations with a rod of iron (Psalms 2:9; Revelation 19:15) take place when he returns. Historic premillennialists such as Ladd agree that Christ reigns now in heaven, but read Revelation 20:4-6 and 1 Corinthians 15:23-24 as allowing an interval between his coming and 'the end' in which his reign is displayed on earth.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers (Hoekema, Riddlebarger, Beale) answer that 1 Corinthians 15:25 says Christ 'must reign until' all enemies are under his feet, so the time of sitting is the time of reigning. Paul places the defeat of death, the last enemy, at the resurrection when Christ comes (1 Corinthians 15:23-26, 54-55), leaving no room for a later age in which death still occurs (compare Isaiah 65:20, which premillennialists apply to the millennium). Hebrews 10:12-13 says Christ sat down after one sacrifice for sins, waiting until his enemies are made his footstool, which presents his priestly and royal work as complete in principle now.
promises.rejoinder: Premillennialists reply that 'then the end' (1 Corinthians 15:24) uses a word ('then', eita) that can allow an interval, just as there has been an interval of nearly two thousand years between 'Christ the firstfruits' and 'those who are Christ's at his coming' (1 Corinthians 15:23). They argue that Revelation 20 supplies that interval. Classic dispensationalists add that Psalms 110:2 locates the rule 'from Zion' and so on earth.

promises.title: The righteous Branch: 'The LORD is our righteousness'
promises.promise: God promises to raise up for David a righteous Branch, who will reign as king, act wisely, and do justice and righteousness in the land. In his days Judah will be saved and Israel will dwell securely, and his name will be 'The LORD is our righteousness'. Jeremiah 33:14-18 repeats the promise and adds that David will never lack a man on the throne of Israel, and the Levitical priests will never lack a man to offer burnt offerings.

path.text: God will raise a righteous Branch for David, a wise king who does justice. His name will be 'The LORD is our righteousness'.
After the exile, Joshua the high priest and his companions are a sign: God will bring his servant the Branch.
God's Son was descended from David according to the flesh and declared Son of God in power by the resurrection.
Christ Jesus became for believers wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. The Branch's name becomes the believer's gift (2 Corinthians 5:21).
Jesus calls himself 'the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star'.

promises.history: Jeremiah spoke this oracle in the last years of Judah, probably under Zedekiah (597-586 BC), whose throne name means 'The LORD is my righteousness'. The promised king's name 'The LORD is our righteousness' contrasts with the failed king and the 'shepherds' condemned in Jeremiah 23:1-2. Zedekiah was the last Davidic king to reign in Jerusalem; he was captured near Jericho and taken to Riblah in 586 BC (Jeremiah 39:4-7). The 'Branch' image is shared with Isaiah 11:1 (a shoot from the stump of Jesse) and Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12. Jeremiah 33:14-26 is missing from the Greek Septuagint, a fact discussed by textual critics.
promises.toUs: Believers are declared righteous because the King is righteous and gives his righteousness to them. The Branch's name is now the confession of every Christian: our righteousness is the LORD himself, in Christ. His wise and just reign is also the pattern for how his people live.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists note that the Branch will 'do justice and righteousness in the land' and that in his days 'Israel will dwell securely' (Jeremiah 23:6), followed by a new exodus 'from the north country' back to 'their own land' (Jeremiah 23:7-8). For Walvoord and Pentecost this describes Christ's earthly reign over a regathered nation, which has not yet happened. Jeremiah 33:17 promises a Davidic king on 'the throne of the house of Israel', which they read as a literal throne in Jerusalem in the millennium.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers point out that Jeremiah 33:18 promises in the same breath that Levitical priests will never lack a man to offer burnt offerings 'continually'. If verse 17 must be literal, verse 18 must be too, but Hebrews teaches that Levitical sacrifice has ended in Christ (Hebrews 7:11-12; 10:11-18). The better reading, Robertson and Gentry and Wellum argue, is that both promises are fulfilled in Christ, who is both David's son and the eternal priest. The new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31-34, given to 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah', is quoted in Hebrews 8:8-12 as fulfilled in Christ's ministry to the church.
promises.rejoinder: Some dispensationalists (Hullinger, Whitcomb) reply that the sacrifices of Jeremiah 33 and Ezekiel 40-48 can be literal in the millennium as memorials or for ceremonial cleansing, not atonement. Progressive dispensationalists (Saucy, Bock) reply that Hebrews applies the new covenant to the church as an inaugurated fulfilment, without cancelling Jeremiah 31:35-37, where Israel's continuance as a nation is as sure as the sun and moon.

promises.title: The fallen tent of David rebuilt, and the nations called by God's name
promises.promise: Amos ends his book of judgment with hope. In that day God will raise up the fallen booth (tent) of David, repair its breaches, and rebuild it as in the days of old, so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that are called by God's name. The book closes with abundant harvests and Israel planted in its land, never again to be uprooted (Amos 9:13-15).

path.text: God will rebuild David's fallen booth, and all the nations called by his name will be included in its rule.
Zechariah praises God for raising up a horn of salvation for us 'in the house of his servant David'.

At the Jerusalem council James says Peter's report of Gentiles believing agrees with the prophets, and quotes Amos 9:11-12 (in a form close to the Greek Old Testament): God rebuilds David's tent so that the rest of mankind, all the Gentiles called by his name, may seek the Lord.
Gentiles are now fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household, built together into a holy temple and a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
The dwelling place ('tabernacle', the same Greek word family as the 'tent' of David in Acts 15:16) of God is with people, and he will dwell with them.

promises.history: Amos prophesied in the days of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, 'two years before the earthquake' (Amos 1:1), around 760 BC; destruction layers at Hazor and other sites are often linked to a large mid-eighth-century earthquake, which Zechariah 14:5 also remembers. Speaking to a prosperous northern kingdom, Amos already called David's house a 'fallen booth', looking ahead to its collapse in 586 BC. Before Christianity, the Qumran community read Amos 9:11 of the coming Branch of David (4Q174) and of the books of the Law (the Damascus Document, CD VII). The Jerusalem council of Acts 15 is usually dated around AD 48-50. James quotes a text close to the Septuagint, which reads 'the rest of men' (Hebrew adam) where the Hebrew has 'Edom'.
promises.toUs: Gentile believers today are part of the rebuilt house of David. James used this text to settle that Gentiles do not need to become Jews (by circumcision) to belong to God's people. The church, Jew and Gentile together, is the place where David's Son now rules and where God dwells.
promises.futurist: Classic dispensationalists, following Scofield and Walvoord, read James's opening words 'After this I will return' (Acts 15:16) as an order of events: first God takes out from the Gentiles a people for his name (Acts 15:14, the church age), and after that Christ returns to rebuild David's tent in the millennium. James only claims that the prophets 'agree' with Gentile salvation, not that Amos is fulfilled now. Progressive dispensationalists such as Bock, and Walter Kaiser in a well-known 1977 article, accept that Acts 15 sees an initial fulfilment now, but hold that Amos 9:14-15 still promises Israel's permanent planting in its land.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers (Robertson, Beale, Holwerda) answer that James's whole argument requires that the rebuilding has begun: the inclusion of Gentiles 'called by my name' is the purpose of the rebuilt tent, so if Gentiles are being included now, the tent is standing now. 'After this I will return' is not in Amos and is probably drawn from texts such as Jeremiah 12:15 or Hosea 3:5 to frame the quotation, not to insert the church age. Richard Bauckham argues that the 'tent of David' was read in Jewish exegesis as the eschatological temple, which James identifies with the community of Jewish and Gentile believers.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists reply that James's point is agreement in principle: God always planned to save Gentiles as Gentiles, which the church shows. This does not prove that the national promises of Amos 9:14-15 ('I will plant them on their land, and they shall never again be uprooted') have been met, especially since Israel was uprooted in AD 70 and AD 135.

promises.title: Ezekiel's temple, the returning glory and the river of life
promises.promise: In Ezekiel 40-48 the prophet is shown a vast temple with exact measurements. The glory of the God of Israel, which had left the temple before its destruction (Ezekiel 10-11), returns from the east and fills the house; God says this is the place of his throne, where he will dwell among Israel forever (Ezekiel 43:1-7). A river flows from the temple, making the Dead Sea fresh and feeding trees whose leaves are for healing (Ezekiel 47:1-12). The land is divided among the twelve tribes in parallel strips, and the city is named 'The LORD is there' (Ezekiel 48:35).

path.text: The glory returns to the temple, and God says he will dwell in the midst of Israel forever.
The returned exiles finish the second temple in the sixth year of Darius and dedicate it with joy. It does not follow Ezekiel's plan, and no return of the glory is recorded.
Jesus cries out that rivers of living water will flow from within whoever believes in him. John explains that he means the Spirit.
Paul says 'we are the temple of the living God' and quotes God's promise to dwell among his people and be their God (Leviticus 26:12; Ezekiel 37:27).
John sees no temple in the new Jerusalem, for the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.
The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations, as in Ezekiel 47:12.

promises.history: Ezekiel 40:1 dates the vision to the twenty-fifth year of the exile, fourteen years after Jerusalem fell, which is 573 BC. The prophet was among the exiles taken to Babylon with Jehoiachin in 597 BC. The second temple, begun under Zerubbabel in 536 BC and completed in 515 BC (Ezra 3:8; 6:15), did not follow Ezekiel's design, and Herod's rebuilding (begun c. 20/19 BC) did not either. Ezekiel's temple therefore has never been built. Jewish interpreters noticed difficulties with it; the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 13b) says that Hananiah ben Hezekiah worked to reconcile Ezekiel's rules with the Law of Moses.
promises.toUs: God's purpose is to dwell with his people, and that purpose is met now in Christ and in the church as God's temple by the Spirit. The river of Ezekiel 47 is the life of the Spirit flowing out through believers to the world. The healing of the nations in Ezekiel 47:12 is the goal of Christian mission and the hope of the new creation.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists such as Feinberg, Pentecost, Walvoord and Hullinger argue that Ezekiel's detailed measurements, gates, chambers and tribal borders demand a literal, future, millennial temple. They answer the problem of animal sacrifices in two main ways: as memorials looking back to the cross (like the Lord's Supper), or, in Hullinger's view, as offerings for ceremonial purity needed because the holy presence of God dwells on an earth still affected by sin. The temple was never built after the exile, so they argue it must still be future.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers (Beale, Block, Hoekema, Robertson) answer that the vision is shown 'in visions of God' on 'a very high mountain' (Ezekiel 40:2), like the symbolic visions earlier in the book. Its sacrifices are said to 'make atonement' (Ezekiel 45:15, 17), the prince offers a sin offering for himself (Ezekiel 45:22), and uncircumcised foreigners are barred (Ezekiel 44:9); a literal return to these after Christ would conflict with Hebrews 10:18 ('there is no longer any offering for sin') and Ephesians 2:14. Revelation 21-22 takes up Ezekiel's images (the high mountain, the measured city, the twelve gates, the river and trees) and fulfils them in a city that has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple.
