promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists reply that the Hebrew word for atonement (kipper) can mean ceremonial cleansing, as it does for objects such as the altar (Ezekiel 43:20, 26), not only forgiveness of sin. They also argue that the order of Revelation 20-22 allows Ezekiel's temple in the millennium (Revelation 20) and no temple in the eternal state (Revelation 21:22). Block, though not a dispensationalist, agrees that Ezekiel's vision is ideological rather than a building plan; dispensationalists see this as a concession that the text is not being read on its own terms.

promises.title: The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former
promises.promise: To the discouraged builders of the second temple, God says that in a little while he will once more shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land, and all nations. The treasures (or 'the desire', KJV) of all nations will come in, and he will fill this house with glory. The silver and gold are his. The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, and in this place he will give peace.

path.text: God will shake heaven, earth and nations, fill the house with glory, and make its latter glory greater than Solomon's.
When the foundation of the second temple is laid, the old men who had seen Solomon's temple weep aloud while others shout for joy.
The infant Jesus is brought into the temple. Simeon calls him God's salvation, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of God's people Israel.
Jesus says, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.' John explains that he spoke of the temple of his body.
Hebrews quotes Haggai 2:6 on the final shaking and says believers are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
The kings of the earth bring their glory into the new Jerusalem, and the glory and honour of the nations are brought into it.

promises.history: Haggai 2:1 dates this word to the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the second year of Darius I, about 17 October 520 BC. The returned exiles had laid the foundation in 536 BC (Ezra 3:8-13) but stopped for about sixteen years; work resumed in 520 BC and the temple was completed in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Later Jewish tradition (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 21b) lists things missing from the second temple, including the ark and the Shekinah glory. Herod the Great rebuilt and enlarged the second temple from his eighteenth year (c. 20/19 BC, Josephus, Antiquities 15.380), and John 2:20 notes it had been under construction for forty-six years when Jesus spoke. Rabbinic writers held that the 'latter glory' was fulfilled in Herod's grand building or in the temple's longer duration; Christian writers held it was fulfilled when the Lord came to his temple (Malachi 3:1).
promises.toUs: The glory that the second temple lacked came in the person of Jesus, who walked in its courts and called his body the true temple. Believers are being built into that greater house. The promise of 'peace in this place' is the peace Christ gives (Ephesians 2:14-17).
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists (Feinberg, Walvoord, Fruchtenbaum) note that Haggai treats the temple on the site as one house through its history ('this house in its former glory', Haggai 2:3). The shaking of the heavens and the overthrow of the thrones of kingdoms (Haggai 2:21-22) have not yet happened in full, so the 'latter glory' will be seen in the millennial temple when Messiah returns to Jerusalem. Christ's visits to Herod's temple were a foretaste, not the fulfilment.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers (Beale, Baldwin, Robertson) answer that Hebrews 12:26-28 interprets Haggai's shaking as the passing of the old order and the giving of an unshakable kingdom, which believers are receiving now. The glory came when God's Son, the true dwelling of God (John 1:14), entered the very temple Haggai spoke to, before it was destroyed in AD 70. A later building on the same site could not be 'this house' in a stronger sense than the house Jesus himself entered.
promises.rejoinder: Future-camp writers reply that Hebrews 12:27 places the removal of shaken things in the future ('yet once more'), so the shaking is not finished. Haggai's promise of peace 'in this place' was not seen when Jesus came, because the same temple was destroyed by Rome within forty years. They therefore expect a final fulfilment at Jerusalem.

promises.title: The Branch will build the temple and sit as priest on his throne
promises.promise: Zechariah is told to make crowns and set one on the head of Joshua the high priest, and to say: here is the man whose name is the Branch. He will branch out from his place and build the temple of the LORD. He will bear royal honour and sit and rule on his throne, and he will be a priest on his throne, with peace between the two offices. Those who are far off will come and help build the temple (Zechariah 6:15).

path.text: The Branch will build the LORD's temple and be both king and priest on one throne.
The hands of Zerubbabel, of David's line, laid the foundation of the house and will finish it. He and Joshua the priest are signs of the coming Branch.
Jesus claims he will raise the temple in three days; John explains that he means his own body, raised from the dead.
Believers have a high priest who sits at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister in the true tent that the Lord set up.
Those once 'far off' are brought near by Christ's blood. With the apostles and prophets as foundation and Christ as cornerstone, they grow into a holy temple in the Lord.
The one who conquers will be made a pillar in the temple of God and will bear the name of the city of God, the new Jerusalem.

promises.history: Zechariah's night visions are dated to the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the second year of Darius I, about February 519 BC (Zechariah 1:7), during the rebuilding of the second temple. Zerubbabel, grandson of King Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:17-19), led the builders, yet the crown in Zechariah 6:11 is set on Joshua the high priest. Under the Mosaic order king and priest were separate offices, and King Uzziah was struck with leprosy for burning incense (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). Zechariah's picture of a priest-king is therefore remarkable. The Qumran community expected two messiahs, one priestly and one royal (1QS IX 11), which shows how unusual it was to unite them.
promises.toUs: Jesus is both the King who rules his people and the Priest who reconciles them to God. He is building his temple now from people far and near, and every believer is a living stone in it (1 Peter 2:4-5). Because he is both, there is 'peace' between God's rule and God's mercy in his work.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Feinberg, Fruchtenbaum) agree that the Branch is the Messiah, but argue that 'he shall build the temple' refers to the millennial temple of Ezekiel 40-48, which he will build after his return. They connect Zechariah 6 with Zechariah 14:16-21, where the surviving nations go up to Jerusalem year by year to worship the King and keep the Feast of Booths. This, they say, describes literal worship in Jerusalem after Christ returns.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers (Beale, Robertson, Baldwin) answer that Jesus himself applies the temple-building role to his resurrection (John 2:19-21), and that the New Testament repeatedly calls the church, gathered around the risen Christ, God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21; 1 Peter 2:5). The note that 'those far off' will help to build (Zechariah 6:15) matches Paul's language for Gentiles brought near (Ephesians 2:13, 17). Christ already sits as priest on his throne (Hebrews 8:1; Psalms 110:4), so the union of offices that Zechariah foresaw has happened.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists reply that Zechariah 14 includes features that are hard to read spiritually: the Mount of Olives split in two (Zechariah 14:4), punishment by drought on nations that do not come up to Jerusalem (14:17-19), and the Feast of Booths kept by Egypt. They argue this requires an earthly kingdom with Jerusalem as its centre.

promises.title: Return after seventy years
promises.promise: Jeremiah wrote to the exiles in Babylon that when seventy years were complete for Babylon, the LORD would visit them and bring them back to Jerusalem. The same letter tells them to build houses, seek the welfare of the city of their exile, and pray for it (Jeremiah 29:5-7). The seventy years are also announced in Jeremiah 25:11-12.

path.text: God fixes a limit to the exile: seventy years for Babylon, then a visit of grace and a return to 'this place'.

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia (538 BC) the LORD stirs Cyrus to issue a decree: the God of heaven has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem, and any of His people may go up. The writer says this happened 'that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled'.

Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years in the first year of Darius the Mede and prays for the city. Gabriel answers with a longer horizon of 'seventy sevens' (Daniel 9:24), so the return from Babylon becomes a pointer to a greater release.
Matthew structures Jesus' genealogy around 'the deportation to Babylon' and 'the Christ'. The exile only truly ends when the Son of David comes to save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).
Peter addresses believers in Asia Minor as 'elect exiles of the dispersion'. The church lives as a people in exile, seeking the good of the city where it lives, as Jeremiah's letter instructed.
The voice from heaven calls, 'Come out of her, my people', as Babylon falls. The final exodus from 'Babylon' ends all exile in the new Jerusalem.

promises.history: Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar in 587/586 BC after earlier deportations in 605 and 597 BC. Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC, and the Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum) records his policy of returning displaced peoples and their gods to their sanctuaries, which matches the setting of Ezra 1. About 42,360 people returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Ezra 2:64), the second temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius I, about 516/515 BC (Ezra 6:15), and Ezra (458/457 BC) and Nehemiah (445/444 BC) followed. Many Jews chose to stay in Babylon, Persia and Egypt, so the Second Temple period had both a restored community in Judea and a wide diaspora.
promises.toUs: The fulfilment reading holds that the return from Babylon proved God keeps his word to the day, but it also left Israel under foreign rule, still waiting for the full end of exile (Nehemiah 9:36-37). That greater return comes through Christ, who forgives the sins that caused exile. Christians are told to live like Jeremiah's exiles: settle, work, pray for the city, and wait for the homecoming (Hebrews 13:14).
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists fully agree that Jeremiah 29:10 was fulfilled literally in 538 BC, and they see this as the model for reading all the return promises. Because God kept the seventy years literally and in the land, they argue, the later promises of a final and permanent return (Jeremiah 30-33; Amos 9:15, 'they shall no more be pulled up') must also be literal and are not yet exhausted. The Babylonian return was partial and temporary; the land was lost again in AD 70 and AD 135, so a final regathering remains.
promises.reply: The fulfilment reading agrees that the return was literal and argues that the New Testament itself presents the deeper, unfinished part of the hope as met in Jesus (Luke 1:68-79; Luke 2:25, 'the consolation of Israel'). The prophets tied the permanent return to a new covenant, a new heart and a Davidic king; these the New Testament says have come (Luke 22:20; Acts 2:30-36). So the literal pattern is real, but its final form is the resurrection people in a renewed creation, not a second political return.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists answer that the fulfilment reading accepts a literal first stage and then changes method for the second. If the seventy years were exact and geographic, consistency suggests the 'no more pulled up' promise (Amos 9:15) will also be geographic. Progressive dispensationalists add that the land can be included in the new creation without being spiritualised away.

promises.title: Regathering from all the nations
promises.promise: Moses foresees Israel scattered among all the nations for covenant unfaithfulness. When they return to the LORD with all their heart, he will gather them even from 'the outermost parts of heaven' and bring them into the land (Deuteronomy 30:1-5), and he will circumcise their heart (30:6). Isaiah 11:11-12 speaks of the Lord recovering his remnant 'a second time' from Assyria, Egypt, Cush, Elam and the coastlands, and Jeremiah 16:14-15 says this gathering will eclipse the exodus from Egypt.

path.text: The gathering follows repentance: the LORD will restore their fortunes and gather them from all the peoples.
The returning assembly of 42,360 under Cyrus is a first, partial gathering, but many tribes and families remain scattered.
The 'root of Jesse' stands as a signal for the peoples, and the nations seek him; Paul quotes this of Christ's ministry to Gentiles in Romans 15:12.
John explains that Jesus would die not for the nation only, but to gather into one the children of God scattered abroad.
At Pentecost, devout Jews 'from every nation under heaven' are gathered in Jerusalem and hear the gospel, and about 3,000 are baptised (Acts 2:41).
The Son of Man sends his angels to gather his elect from the four winds, the final regathering.

promises.history: By the first century the Jewish diaspora was larger than the population of Judea: there were large communities in Babylonia, Alexandria in Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor and Rome. Luke's list in Acts 2:9-11 (Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya near Cyrene, Rome, Crete and Arabia) reads like a map of that diaspora, and it overlaps strikingly with the lands named in Isaiah 11:11. Pilgrims came to Jerusalem for the great feasts, so Pentecost brought the scattered people to Zion.
promises.toUs: On the fulfilment reading, the regathering is completed as Jesus gathers the scattered people of God, Jew first and then Gentile, into one flock around himself. Deuteronomy 30:6 (a circumcised heart) is the inner condition, and Paul applies heart circumcision to all believers (Romans 2:28-29; Colossians 2:11). Believers today are part of the gathering, and they join in it by mission to every nation.
promises.futurist: Dispensational writers such as Walvoord and Fruchtenbaum argue that Isaiah 11:11 speaks of a 'second' worldwide regathering, the first being from Babylon, and that the return of Jews since the late nineteenth century and the founding of the State of Israel in 1948 begin it. Fruchtenbaum distinguishes a regathering in unbelief, in preparation for judgment (Ezekiel 20:33-38; Zephaniah 2:1-2), from a final regathering in faith after Messiah returns. They note that the promise is to the land given to the fathers (Deuteronomy 30:5), which a spiritual reading cannot satisfy.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers reply that Isaiah 11:16 explains 'second time' by comparison with the exodus from Egypt, so the first gathering is the exodus and the second is the post-exilic and messianic gathering, not a twentieth-century event. Deuteronomy 30:1-2 places the return after heartfelt return to the LORD, while the founding of the modern state was led mainly by a secular national movement. The New Testament applies the gathering language to Jesus' mission (John 11:52) and to Pentecost, and does not point to a later political return.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists answer that Ezekiel 36:24-27 and 37:7-10 put the physical gathering before the cleansing and the giving of the Spirit, so a return in unbelief fits the order. They argue that John 11:52 adds the Gentiles without cancelling the land promise, and that Jesus himself spoke of Jerusalem being trampled 'until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled' (Luke 21:24), which implies a change for Jerusalem afterwards.

promises.title: The valley of dry bones and the two sticks
promises.promise: Ezekiel sees a valley of very dry bones. At the prophetic word they come together and are covered with flesh, and then breath (ruach) enters them and they stand as a great army (Ezekiel 37:7-10). God explains that the bones are 'the whole house of Israel', who say 'our hope is lost', and promises to open their graves, put his Spirit in them and bring them into the land (37:11-14). The sign of the two sticks follows: Judah and Joseph (Ephraim) will become one nation under one king, 'David my servant', one shepherd, with an everlasting covenant of peace and God's sanctuary among them for ever (37:15-28).

path.text: God promises to open the graves of his people and bring them into the land of Israel, so that they know he is the LORD.

At the dedication of the second temple the returned exiles offer twelve male goats 'according to the number of the tribes of Israel'. The small community sees itself as all Israel restored, a first sign of the two sticks joined.

The risen Jesus breathes on his disciples and says 'Receive the Holy Spirit'. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb (emphysao) in Ezekiel 37:9 and Genesis 2:7, so new creation life comes from the risen king.
Jesus, the good shepherd, says there will be 'one flock, one shepherd', which echoes Ezekiel 37:24 and 34:23.
Christ makes 'one new man' from Jew and Gentile and reconciles both in one body through the cross, which the fulfilment reading sees as the widest form of the two sticks becoming one.
The dwelling of God is with people; Ezekiel 37:27 ('my dwelling place shall be with them') is finally realised in the new creation, after the bodily resurrection.

promises.history: Ezekiel prophesied among the deportees by the Chebar canal in Babylonia from 593 BC. The northern kingdom (Ephraim) had been taken by Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6), and Judah's temple fell in 586 BC, so 'our bones are dried up' was the exiles' own lament. The 'ten lost tribes' were not wholly lost: people from the north joined Judah at different times (2 Chronicles 30:11; 2 Chronicles 34:9), and the New Testament mentions Anna 'of the tribe of Asher' (Luke 2:36) and 'our twelve tribes' (Acts 26:7). Second Temple Jews still longed for a full reunion and the resurrection, which Daniel 12:2 also promised.
promises.toUs: The fulfilment reading holds that Ezekiel 37 is fulfilled in stages: the return from exile, the resurrection of Jesus and the gift of the Spirit, the new birth of believers (Ephesians 2:1-5), and the final bodily resurrection. The text shows that a people can be restored only by God's word and Spirit. Believers, Jew and Gentile, are one flock under one shepherd, and Paul quotes Ezekiel 37:27 about the church as God's temple (2 Corinthians 6:16).
promises.futurist: Many dispensationalists see the founding of Israel in 1948 as bones coming together 'without breath' (Ezekiel 37:8): a nation formed in unbelief, awaiting the Spirit at Christ's return. They stress the concrete details: the land of Israel (37:12, 37:21), one nation on 'the mountains of Israel' (37:22), and the end of the north-south split, which they say no church-age event has satisfied. The sanctuary 'in their midst for evermore' (37:26-28) leads into the temple vision of Ezekiel 40-48, which they expect in the millennium.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers answer that 37:11 explains the bones as the exiles' despair in the sixth century BC, not as a twentieth-century state, and that Paul and Jesus explicitly use the passage's covenant and shepherd language for the church (2 Corinthians 6:16; John 10:16). The text's own order is word and Spirit first, then life; a nation formed by a secular movement does not match a resurrection by the Spirit. The 'everlasting' sanctuary is the presence of God in Christ and his people (John 2:19-21), completed in Revelation 21:22.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists reply that Ezekiel 37:7-8 shows two stages, bones assembled and then breath, so a gathering before spiritual life is in the text. They hold that the church's share in the blessings of the new covenant does not exhaust the specific promise of one nation in the land under the Davidic king, and they point to Romans 11:26-27 as a future national conversion that would complete the picture.

promises.title: The new covenant
promises.promise: The LORD promises a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant broken after the exodus. He will put his law within them and write it on their hearts; all will know him, from least to greatest; and he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more. The following verses (31:35-37) say Israel will not cease as a nation before God while sun and moon remain.

path.text: God will write his law on their hearts and be their God, and they will be his people.
Moses sprinkles 'the blood of the covenant' at Sinai, the pattern that the new covenant both echoes and surpasses.
At the Last Supper Jesus calls the cup 'the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you'.

Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 in full and says Jesus is mediator of this 'better covenant' (8:6). Hebrews 8:13 adds that the first covenant is 'becoming obsolete and growing old' and is 'ready to vanish away'.
Paul calls himself and his co-workers 'ministers of a new covenant', written by the Spirit 'on tablets of human hearts' (3:3).
Believers have come to 'Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant', within the heavenly Jerusalem that will be fully revealed at the end.

promises.history: Jeremiah gave this word around the fall of Jerusalem (587/586 BC), when the Sinai covenant's curses had fallen. In the Second Temple period the Qumran community called itself the people of 'the new covenant in the land of Damascus' (Damascus Document), showing that Jews of Jesus' time longed for it. Jesus' words at the Passover meal, in Jerusalem about AD 30 or 33, claim that it is inaugurated by his death. Hebrews, written probably before AD 70 (disputed), says the old order is 'ready to vanish', and the temple and its sacrifices ended with the Roman destruction in AD 70.
promises.toUs: On the fulfilment reading, every believer, Jew or Gentile, is already a member of the new covenant made 'with the house of Israel', because they are in Christ, the true Israel. This is why the Lord's Supper is called the new covenant (1 Corinthians 11:25), and why Christians have full forgiveness, the indwelling Spirit and direct knowledge of God. The covenant's promises are the believer's present inheritance, not a later Jewish dispensation.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists stress that Jeremiah names the parties: the house of Israel and the house of Judah, and they link it to Israel's continuing national existence in 31:35-37. Classic dispensationalists held various views (Chafer once proposed two new covenants; Ryrie and Walvoord teach one covenant whose spiritual blessings the church shares now while its national and land aspects await Israel). Progressive dispensationalists such as Blaising, Bock and Saucy say the covenant is inaugurated at the cross but will be fully realised when 'all Israel' is saved (Romans 11:26-27 quotes Isaiah 59:21 and Jeremiah 31:34).
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers answer that Hebrews applies the very text, including 'house of Israel', to its Christian readers without any hint of a later second stage for the nation. Since Gentiles are grafted into Israel's olive tree (Romans 11:17), the covenant with 'Israel' includes them. Jeremiah 31:35-37 is fulfilled in the continuing existence of Israel as the remnant and the Messiah's people, who will never cease (Matthew 16:18).
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists answer that Hebrews 8 shows the covenant has begun, not that Israel's national role is ended. Romans 11:27 places the covenant's removal of Israel's sins in connection with a future saving of 'all Israel' after 'the fullness of the Gentiles has come in' (11:25). They hold that a covenant can be inaugurated with Gentile participants while its national promises await the nation.

promises.title: A new heart and a new spirit
promises.promise: God will take Israel from the nations and bring them into their own land, sprinkle clean water on them and cleanse them from idols, give them a new heart and a new spirit, remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh, and put his Spirit within them so that they walk in his statutes (Ezekiel 36:24-27). Then they will dwell in the land and be his people (36:28). God says he acts for the sake of his holy name, which Israel had profaned among the nations (36:22).

path.text: God promises a new heart and a new spirit, replacing the heart of stone.
The returned exiles, with those who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the nations, keep the Passover: a first, partial cleansing.
Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one enters God's kingdom unless born 'of water and the Spirit', and rebukes the 'teacher of Israel' for not knowing it (3:10), which points to Ezekiel 36:25-27.
The exalted Jesus pours out the promised Holy Spirit on Jews gathered from the nations at Pentecost.
Paul says the Corinthians are a letter of Christ written by the Spirit 'on tablets of human hearts' (literally hearts of flesh), echoing Ezekiel 36:26.
The one who overcomes will inherit all things; God will be his God and he will be God's son, the covenant formula completed.

promises.history: Ezekiel spoke this after news of Jerusalem's fall reached the exiles (Ezekiel 33:21, about 585 BC). After the return, the reforms of Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 9-10; Nehemiah 8-10) show both a real turning to the law and repeated failure (Nehemiah 13), so the 'new heart' was still awaited. At Pentecost in Jerusalem, the Spirit came on Jews 'from every nation under heaven' (Acts 2:5), the very people taken from the nations that Ezekiel had described, and Peter then offered the Spirit to 'all who are far off' (Acts 2:39).
promises.toUs: The fulfilment reading holds that every Christian has received what Ezekiel promised: cleansing, a new heart and the indwelling Spirit (Titus 3:5; Romans 8:9). Obedience is the fruit of this inner change, not its cause. Because Gentiles receive the same Spirit (Acts 10:44-47; Acts 15:8-9), they share in the restoration that Ezekiel promised to Israel.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists point to the order in Ezekiel 36:24-25: first God takes Israel from the nations into its own land, then he sprinkles clean water. They see a regathering in unbelief (beginning in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries) followed by a national new birth at Christ's return (Zechariah 12:10; Romans 11:26). The church receives the Spirit now, but the promise to the nation in its land, with 'the cities inhabited and the waste places rebuilt' (36:33-35), is still future.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers answer that the New Testament places the giving of this Spirit at Pentecost, to Jews gathered in Jerusalem from the nations, so the order of Ezekiel 36 has already been enacted. The new heart cannot be given to a nation as a political unit; it is given to persons who believe, whether Jew or Gentile. The rebuilt cities and fruitful land are, in this view, fulfilled typologically after the exile and finally in the renewed earth.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists reply that Pentecost was a real beginning but not the national, complete renewal described: 'I will save you from all your uncleanness' (36:29) concerns 'the house of Israel' as a whole (36:22, 36:32). Paul's hope for 'all Israel' (Romans 11:26) confirms, they say, that the nation's corporate renewal is still ahead.

promises.title: The Spirit poured out on all flesh
promises.promise: After a plague of locusts and a call to repentance, God promises that 'afterward' he will pour out his Spirit on all flesh: sons and daughters will prophesy, old men dream, young men see visions, even servants receive the Spirit. There will be wonders in heaven and earth, the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the great day of the LORD, and whoever calls on the name of the LORD will be saved, with deliverance in Mount Zion and Jerusalem (Joel 2:32).

path.text: God will pour his Spirit on all flesh, without distinction of age, sex or social rank.
Moses wished that all the LORD's people were prophets and that he would put his Spirit on them; Joel promises exactly this.
John the Baptist says the coming one will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire.
Peter says 'this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel' and quotes the whole passage, adding 'in the last days'.
Paul quotes Joel 2:32 ('everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved') and applies it to Jew and Greek alike (10:12), with 'Lord' meaning Jesus (10:9).
The Spirit and the bride say 'Come'; the Spirit-filled people call the world until the final day of the Lord.

promises.history: Joel's date is disputed (proposals range from the ninth to the fourth century BC). The fulfilment happened at the feast of Weeks (Shavuot, Pentecost) in Jerusalem around AD 30 or 33, when Jewish pilgrims and proselytes from Parthia to Rome were present (Acts 2:9-11) and about 3,000 believed (Acts 2:41). Peter adds 'to all who are far off' (Acts 2:39), and the same Spirit later falls on Samaritans (Acts 8:17) and on the Gentile household of Cornelius (Acts 10:44-45). Within a generation, in AD 70, Jerusalem itself fell, which many fulfilment writers connect with the 'great and awesome day' that Peter warned about (Acts 2:40, 'this crooked generation').
promises.toUs: On the fulfilment reading, the church lives in Joel's 'last days': every believer has the Spirit and shares the prophetic calling to speak of God's works. The 'all flesh' of Joel is shown to include the Gentiles. The promise of rescue to 'whoever calls on the name of the LORD' is the basis of evangelism to every nation today.
promises.futurist: Some dispensationalists, including Fruchtenbaum, hold that Acts 2 is an application or a partial fulfilment, because the signs of Joel 2:30-31 (blood, fire, darkened sun, blood-red moon) did not occur visibly at Pentecost. They note that Joel's context is Israel's land and harvest restored (2:18-27) and the nations judged in the valley of Jehoshaphat (Joel 3), which they place at the end of the tribulation. Progressive dispensationalists, such as Bock, accept a real initial fulfilment at Pentecost while expecting the cosmic signs and full national blessing at Christ's return.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers note that Peter does not say 'this is like' but 'this is what was spoken' (Acts 2:16) and quotes the signs too. Cosmic darkening is a standard prophetic image for the fall of a power (Isaiah 13:10 for Babylon; Ezekiel 32:7 for Egypt), and the darkness at the crucifixion (Luke 23:44-45) and the judgment of AD 70 fit the 'day' Peter warns of. Paul's use of Joel 2:32 for Gentiles in Romans 10 shows that 'Zion' deliverance is now through faith in Jesus.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists answer that an 'already, not yet' fulfilment, which progressive dispensationalists accept, still leaves room for future events: the cosmic signs appear again in Jesus' teaching about his coming (Matthew 24:29) and in Revelation 6:12. They hold that Joel 3:1 ('when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem') ties the outpouring to a national restoration that is still future.

promises.title: The nations stream to Zion
promises.promise: In the latter days the mountain of the LORD's house will be raised above the hills, and all nations will flow to it, saying 'Let us go up to the mountain of the LORD' to learn his ways. Instruction (torah) will go out from Zion and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem; he will judge between nations, and they will beat swords into ploughshares and learn war no more. Micah 4:1-3 gives almost the same oracle.

path.text: Many peoples come to Zion to be taught, and the word of the LORD goes out from Jerusalem.
Solomon prays that foreigners who come because of God's great name will be heard when they pray toward the temple, so that all peoples may know him.
The risen Jesus says repentance and forgiveness will be proclaimed in his name to all nations, 'beginning from Jerusalem'; the word goes out from Zion.
The witnesses go from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria and the end of the earth.
Believers 'have come to Mount Zion', the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem; the nations now come to Zion by coming to Christ.
The nations walk by the light of the new Jerusalem and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it.

promises.history: Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, when the temple mount was small and Judah was threatened by Assyria. In the Second Temple period Herod's rebuilt temple (begun about 20/19 BC) had a large Court of the Gentiles, and many Gentile 'God-fearers' attached themselves to synagogues (Acts 10:2; Acts 13:16), while proselytes came on pilgrimage (Acts 2:10; the Ethiopian official in Acts 8:27). After Pentecost the gospel went out from Jerusalem to Samaria (Acts 8), Antioch (Acts 11:20-21) and Rome, and in AD 70 the temple itself was destroyed.
promises.toUs: The fulfilment reading holds that Christians from the nations are the peoples who have 'gone up' to Zion, by coming to Jesus and learning his ways. The word from Zion is the gospel, and every believer joins in sending it to the nations. The beating of swords into ploughshares has begun in the reconciled community of the church (Ephesians 2:14-17) and will be complete when Christ judges the nations at the end.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists read this as a picture of the millennial kingdom: Christ will reign from a literal, physically exalted Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:10 speaks of the land levelled and Jerusalem raised), the nations will go up to it (Zechariah 14:16), and world disarmament will occur. They point out that universal peace has clearly not arrived in history, so the passage must refer to a future age on this earth, before the eternal state.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers answer that the 'latter days' are the days begun with Christ (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), and that Jesus expressly told the Samaritan woman that worship would no longer be tied to 'this mountain' or Jerusalem (John 4:21-23). The law going out from Zion fits the apostolic mission, which Luke frames 'beginning from Jerusalem'. Amillennialists place full world peace in the new creation; postmillennialists expect it to grow through the gospel within history, as the kingdom spreads (Matthew 13:31-33).
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists reply that the promise includes nations still learning and being judged (2:4), which fits a millennial age better than the eternal state, where no one needs arbitration. They argue that Hebrews 12:22 describes believers' present access to heaven, not a cancellation of the earthly Jerusalem's future role, and that Jesus himself spoke of Jerusalem's future 'until' the times of the Gentiles end (Luke 21:24).

promises.title: A light to the nations
promises.promise: The Servant, whom God calls 'Israel' (Isaiah 49:3), is given a mission to raise up the tribes of Jacob and restore the preserved of Israel. God says that is too small a thing: he will also make the Servant a light to the nations, so that his salvation reaches the end of the earth (49:6).

path.text: God calls his Servant 'Israel', in whom he will be glorified, yet this Servant also restores Israel (49:5).
God's promise to Abraham that in him all families of the earth will be blessed is the root of Israel's calling to the nations.
Simeon takes the infant Jesus in the temple and calls him 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel'.
At Pisidian Antioch, Paul and Barnabas quote Isaiah 49:6 and say 'the Lord has commanded us' with it, turning to the Gentiles.
Paul tells Agrippa that the Messiah, first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light both to the Jewish people and to the Gentiles.
A great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language stands before the throne and the Lamb.

promises.history: Isaiah 40-55 addresses the exiles in Babylon, promising return and naming Cyrus (Isaiah 44:28; 45:1). The return under Cyrus (538 BC) restored some of 'the preserved of Israel', but no light reached the nations in any great way. In the first century, synagogues across the Roman world drew Gentile God-fearers, and Paul's mission, beginning about AD 46-48 in Cyprus and Galatia (Acts 13-14), made this text his commission. By the time Paul wrote Romans (about AD 57) there were churches of Gentiles from Jerusalem to Illyricum (Romans 15:19).
promises.toUs: The fulfilment reading holds that Jesus is the true Israel and the Servant who restores the remnant of Jacob and also lights the nations. Because the apostles apply the Servant's mission to themselves (Acts 13:47), the church shares in it: Jew and Gentile believers carry the light of Israel's Messiah to the end of the earth. Gentile Christians are therefore the fruit of Israel's calling, not outsiders to it.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists agree that the Servant is the Messiah and that the Gentile mission fulfils part of Isaiah 49:6. They stress that the restoration of 'the tribes of Jacob' (49:6) and the land (49:8, 'to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages') is still ahead. They expect national Israel, once converted, to be a light to the nations in the millennium (Isaiah 60:3; Zechariah 8:23, where ten men from the nations take hold of a Jew's robe).
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers reply that the restoration of Jacob's tribes began with Jesus' choice of the Twelve (Luke 22:30) and the thousands of Jews who believed (Acts 21:20). The land-apportioning image in 49:8 is quoted by Paul for the present day of salvation ('now is the day of salvation', 2 Corinthians 6:2 quoting Isaiah 49:8), so the passage's time is the gospel age. In Zechariah 8:23 the nations seek out the Jew because 'God is with you', which they see fulfilled when Gentiles came to Jewish apostles and their Messiah.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists answer that a present application does not exhaust a text: Paul can quote Isaiah 49:8 for today while the nation's land restoration still awaits. They argue that Romans 11:12 ('how much more their fullness') shows a greater blessing to the nations when Israel as a people turns to Christ.

promises.title: 'Not my people' called 'my people'
promises.promise: Hosea's children were named Lo-ruhamah ('no mercy') and Lo-ammi ('not my people') as signs of judgment on the northern kingdom (Hosea 1:6-9). Yet God promises that the number of Israel will be like the sand of the sea, and where it was said 'You are not my people', they will be called 'children of the living God' (1:10). Judah and Israel will be gathered under one head (1:11), and God will say to 'not my people', 'You are my people' (2:23).

path.text: God will have mercy on 'no mercy' and say to 'not my people', 'You are my people'.
Hosea buys back his unfaithful wife, a picture of Israel returning in the latter days to seek the LORD and 'David their king'.
Those once far off are brought near by the blood of Christ.
Paul says God has called vessels of mercy 'not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles', and quotes Hosea 2:23 and 1:10 as the proof.
Peter tells his readers: once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have.
'They will be his people, and God himself will be with them': the covenant formula is fulfilled for the whole redeemed humanity.

promises.history: Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom in the eighth century BC, before Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6). Assyria resettled the northern Israelites among the nations and brought foreigners into Samaria (2 Kings 17:24), so the 'not my people' became mixed among the Gentiles. Paul wrote Romans about AD 57 to a church of Jewish and Gentile believers in Rome, where Jews had been expelled under Claudius about AD 49 and had since returned (Acts 18:2). 1 Peter's readers in Asia Minor seem to have been largely Gentile (1 Peter 1:18; 4:3), though this is disputed.
promises.toUs: The fulfilment reading holds that Gentile believers are the 'not my people' who have become 'my people' and 'children of the living God'. This is one of the clearest places where the New Testament applies a promise made to Israel directly to Gentiles. Christians therefore receive Israel's covenant titles (1 Peter 2:9-10: chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation) by mercy, not by birth.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists such as Vlach note that in Hosea the promise concerns the northern tribes of Israel, and that Hosea 1:11 and 3:5 add a reunited people under David in the land. They hold that Paul and Peter use Hosea by analogy: the same God who calls rejected Israel 'my people' can call Gentiles who were never his people. The Gentile application shows God's character but does not remove the original promise to ethnic Israel, which remains for a future national restoration.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers answer that Paul introduces the text as 'as indeed he says in Hosea' (Romans 9:25), which grounds his claim, not merely illustrates it. Since the northern tribes were scattered and mixed among the nations, some writers see the Gentile mission as gathering the very people Hosea described. Either way, the New Testament treats the Hosea promise as now being fulfilled in a mixed Jewish-Gentile church.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists reply that Paul next turns to Isaiah's remnant texts for Israel (Romans 9:27-29), keeping a distinction between Israel and the Gentiles inside the argument. They point out that Romans 11:1-2 denies that God has rejected his people, which they take as a continuing national promise beside the Gentile one.

promises.title: The remnant will return
promises.promise: In the day of Assyria's judgment, 'a remnant will return' (shear yashub), the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God. Though Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return; destruction is decreed, overflowing with righteousness (Isaiah 10:20-22). The name of Isaiah's son Shear-jashub (Isaiah 7:3) means 'a remnant will return'.

path.text: A remnant of Jacob will return to the mighty God.
In Elijah's day God kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal; Paul uses this example in Romans 11:4.
Jesus calls his disciples 'little flock' and promises them the kingdom; the faithful remnant gathers around him.
Paul quotes Isaiah 10:22: though Israel's number be as the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved.
'At the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace'; Paul himself, an Israelite of Benjamin, is evidence (11:1).
'And in this way all Israel will be saved'; how the remnant relates to 'all Israel' is the central question of the debate.

promises.history: Isaiah spoke during the Assyrian crisis, when the north fell (722 BC) and Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BC, taking many cities and besieging Jerusalem, as his own annals (the Taylor Prism) also record. Only Jerusalem survived, 'a remnant' (2 Kings 19:30-31). In the first century, the Jewish believers in Jesus numbered 'many thousands' in Jerusalem (Acts 21:20), but most of the nation's leaders rejected him, and Paul wrestles with this in Romans 9-11 about AD 57, a decade before the war with Rome.
promises.toUs: On the fulfilment reading, the true Israel has always been the believing remnant within the nation, and Gentiles are grafted into that remnant (Romans 11:17). The church is not a new people replacing Israel but the faithful remnant of Israel enlarged with Gentiles. This keeps believers humble: they stand by faith, not by birth (Romans 11:20).
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists see the present Jewish remnant in the church as a pledge that God has not finished with Israel as a nation. Paul says Israel's 'fullness' (11:12) and 'acceptance' (11:15) will bring 'life from the dead' to the world, and that a partial hardening lasts 'until' the fullness of the Gentiles comes in (11:25). They read 'all Israel' in 11:26 as the nation at the end of the age, turning to Christ at his return.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers are divided here. Robertson and many amillennialists read 'and in this way' (houtos, 11:26) as describing the manner: all the elect of Israel are saved through history as remnant after remnant believes alongside the Gentiles. Others in the Reformed tradition, such as Hodge, Vos and John Murray, expect a future large-scale turning of ethnic Jews to Christ, but without a restored national kingdom or a separate land program. Both hold that any future conversion brings Jews into the one olive tree, the church.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists answer that the 'until' of 11:25 and the contrast between Israel's present 'trespass' and future 'fullness' (11:12) imply a change of condition for the same Israel that is now hardened, that is, ethnic Israel. They welcome the Murray-Vos reading as partial agreement and argue that Romans 11:28-29 ('the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable', said of those who are now enemies of the gospel) points to more than individual conversion.

promises.title: Zion, the mother city of the nations
promises.promise: Psalm 87 names Rahab (Egypt), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush among those who know the LORD, and says of each, 'this one was born there'; the LORD registers the peoples as born in Zion (Psalms 87:4-6). Isaiah 60 sees nations coming to Zion's light, its gates open day and night to receive their wealth, and the LORD himself as its everlasting light so that sun and moon are no longer needed (Isaiah 60:3, 60:11, 60:19).

path.text: Of Zion it will be said that this one and that one were born in her, and the Most High establishes her.
David captures the stronghold of Zion, which becomes the city of David and the seat of the Davidic king (Psalms 2:6).
Jesus enters Jerusalem as the king who comes to the daughter of Zion, humble and riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9).
Paul says 'the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother', contrasting it with 'the present Jerusalem' which is in slavery with her children (4:25).
Believers have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, which echoes the registry of Psalm 87.
John sees the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven; it has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God is its light (21:23), as Isaiah 60:19 foretold.

promises.history: Zion was the Jebusite fortress that David took around 1000 BC. After the exile, Nehemiah rebuilt the walls in 445/444 BC in 52 days (Nehemiah 6:15), and Herod the Great later made Jerusalem one of the grand cities of the East. Paul wrote Galatians (late 40s or early 50s AD, disputed) against teachers who pressed Gentile believers to take on circumcision, and he called the earthly Jerusalem of his day a city 'in slavery'. In AD 70 the Romans under Titus destroyed the city and temple; after the Bar Kokhba revolt (AD 132-135) Hadrian refounded it as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina and barred Jews from it.
promises.toUs: On the fulfilment reading, every believer, whatever their birth, is enrolled as 'born in Zion' and is a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem (Philippians 3:20; Ephesians 2:19). Christians come to Zion now in worship, and they wait for the city that will come down at the end. Love for Zion means love for the people of God from every nation, gathered around the King.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists hold that Isaiah 60 describes a restored earthly Jerusalem in the millennium: foreigners rebuild its walls (60:10), the descendants of its oppressors bow at its feet (60:14), and it is called 'the City of the LORD, the Zion of the Holy One of Israel' (60:14). They see the heavenly Jerusalem of Revelation 21 as the eternal city after the millennium, distinct from the earthly capital of the thousand years. Many see the reunification of Jerusalem under Israeli rule in 1967 as connected with Luke 21:24 ('until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled'), though others in the camp are cautious about such links.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers reply that Revelation 21-22 quotes Isaiah 60 again and again (the light, the open gates, the nations' glory), which places its fulfilment in the new Jerusalem rather than an intermediate city. Paul's contrast of the 'present Jerusalem' and the 'Jerusalem above' (Galatians 4:25-26) leaves no theological future for the earthly city as such. Psalm 87 already sees Zion as a city whose citizens are born from the nations, which is the church's identity.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists answer that Revelation 21 can draw on Isaiah 60 for the eternal state while Isaiah 60's details of foreign kings, enemies bowing and walls built by foreigners fit an earthly age better. They argue that Galatians 4 is about two covenants (law and promise), not about the future of Jerusalem as a place, and point to Jesus' words that Jerusalem will not see him 'until' it says 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' (Matthew 23:39).

promises.title: Daniel's seventy weeks
promises.promise: While praying about Jeremiah's seventy years, Daniel is told by Gabriel that seventy 'sevens' are decreed for his people and his holy city: to finish transgression, end sins, atone for iniquity, bring in everlasting righteousness, seal vision and prophet, and anoint a most holy place (Daniel 9:24). From a word to restore Jerusalem to an anointed one there will be seven and sixty-two sevens; then an anointed one will be cut off, and the people of a coming prince will destroy the city and sanctuary (9:25-26). 'He' will confirm a covenant with many for one seven and in the middle of it end sacrifice and offering, with an abomination that desolates (9:27).

path.text: Six goals are set within seventy sevens for Daniel's people and holy city.
The jubilee came after seven sevens of years; seventy sevens are ten jubilees, a final release beyond the seventy years of exile (Jeremiah 25:11).
Jesus begins his ministry announcing 'the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near'.
Jesus speaks of 'my blood of the covenant, poured out for many', which fulfilment writers connect with the covenant confirmed 'with many' (Daniel 9:27).
Christ has appeared once at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself, the 'end of sins' and 'atonement for iniquity' of Daniel 9:24.
Jesus refers to 'the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel'; fulfilment writers place it in AD 66-70 (compare Luke 21:20), futurists in a coming tribulation.

promises.history: Gabriel's word came in the first year of Darius the Mede (Daniel 9:1), about 539 BC. Possible starting points are Cyrus' decree (538 BC, Ezra 1:1-4), Artaxerxes' commission to Ezra (458/457 BC, Ezra 7), and Artaxerxes' permission to Nehemiah to rebuild the city (445/444 BC, Nehemiah 2:1-8). From 457 BC, 483 years reach about AD 26-27, near Jesus' baptism; Sir Robert Anderson and later Harold Hoehner counted from 444 BC with 360-day prophetic years to AD 32 or 33. Jesus was crucified about AD 30 or 33, and Roman legions under Titus destroyed the city and temple in AD 70, as Daniel 9:26 described.
promises.toUs: The fulfilment reading (Young, Kline, Robertson, Gentry) holds that the six goals of 9:24 are accomplished by Christ's death and resurrection: sin ended, atonement made, everlasting righteousness brought in. The 'he' of 9:27 is the Messiah, who confirms the covenant with many and makes the temple sacrifices obsolete by his own sacrifice, while the 'people of the prince', the Romans, destroy the city in AD 70. Believers live in the righteousness that Daniel's weeks promised, and the fall of the temple shows that sacrifice has ended for ever.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Hoehner, Ice) argue that the sixty-nine weeks ended at Jesus' triumphal entry or crucifixion, after which the prophetic clock stopped. Verse 26 places the cutting off of Messiah and the destruction of AD 70 'after' the sixty-two weeks, not inside the seventieth, so a gap is in the text. The 'he' of 9:27 is the nearest antecedent, 'the prince who is to come', a future Antichrist who will make a seven-year treaty with Israel and break it in the middle, matching the 42 months and 1,260 days of Revelation 11:2 and 12:6 and the man of lawlessness in the temple (2 Thessalonians 2:4).
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers answer that nothing in the text suggests a gap of two thousand years inside a numbered sequence, and that the main subject of 9:25-26 is the Messiah, not the prince, who is only mentioned in a phrase about his 'people'. Confirming a covenant 'with many' fits the new covenant (Isaiah 53:11-12 'he shall justify many'; Matthew 26:28), not a peace treaty, and Jesus' ministry of about three and a half years before his death fits 'the middle of the week'. Some (Kline) read the seventieth week symbolically as stretching through the church age to the end.
promises.rejoinder: Futurists reply that Jesus placed the abomination of desolation in the future in his own teaching (Matthew 24:15), and the events after it include his coming in glory (24:29-31), which did not happen in AD 70. The six goals of 9:24 include 'to seal up vision and prophecy' and full everlasting righteousness for Daniel's people and city, which they argue are not yet complete for Israel. Prophetic gaps elsewhere (Isaiah 61:1-2 read by Jesus in Luke 4:18-19, stopping before 'the day of vengeance') show the pattern is not foreign to Scripture.

promises.title: They will look on him whom they pierced
promises.promise: God will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and supplication, and they will look on 'me whom they have pierced' and mourn for him as for an only son (Zechariah 12:10). The mourning is likened to the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo (12:11), and on that day a fountain will be opened for sin and uncleanness (13:1).

path.text: Jerusalem will look on the pierced one and mourn, after God pours out a spirit of grace.
The great lament for King Josiah, killed at Megiddo, became a lasting national mourning, the pattern Zechariah 12:11 recalls.
After the soldier pierces Jesus' side, John says 'another Scripture says, They will look on him whom they pierced'.
At Pentecost, after the Spirit is poured out, Jerusalem's crowds are 'cut to the heart' about the Jesus they crucified (2:36) and about 3,000 repent.
The blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin, the fountain of Zechariah 13:1 opened for believers.
He comes with the clouds, every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth (or land) will mourn.

promises.history: Zechariah prophesied in Jerusalem from 520 BC (Zechariah 1:1), encouraging the rebuilding of the second temple under Zerubbabel. The mourning for Josiah, killed by Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:29), was still remembered as the nation's great grief. Jesus was crucified by Roman soldiers at the request of Jerusalem's leaders around AD 30 or 33, and John, writing later in the century, presents himself as the eyewitness of the piercing (John 19:35). Revelation, dated either before AD 70 or about AD 95 (disputed), applies the text to Christ's coming.
promises.toUs: The fulfilment reading holds that the piercing was fulfilled at the cross and the looking and mourning began at Pentecost, when the Spirit of grace was poured out and Jews in Jerusalem repented. Every believer has 'looked' on the pierced one in faith and found the cleansing fountain. Revelation 1:7 widens the circle: at his coming all will see him, and those who did not repent will mourn in judgment.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists (Fruchtenbaum, Walvoord, Ice) read Zechariah 12-14 as one end-time scene: all nations gather against Jerusalem (12:2-3, 12:9), God defends the city, and the nation as a whole, by families and clans (12:12-14), turns to the Messiah at his visible return. They connect this to Hosea 5:15, Matthew 23:39 and Romans 11:26 as Israel's national confession that precedes or accompanies the second coming. John 19:37 fulfils the piercing; the national mourning is still future.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers answer that John explicitly ties the text to the crucifixion, and Acts shows the outpouring of the Spirit and the mourning of Jerusalem's people in Acts 2. Preterists read Revelation 1:7's 'tribes of the land' as Judea's tribes seeing Christ's coming in the judgment of AD 70; amillennialists see the final universal coming, when all, including the unrepentant, will mourn. Neither reading needs a distinct national conversion inside a future political state.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists reply that Acts 2 involved thousands, not the clan-by-clan mourning of the whole house of David and of Jerusalem in 12:12-14. They hold that the setting, with all nations besieging Jerusalem and God destroying them (12:9), did not occur at Pentecost or at AD 70, when Jerusalem fell rather than being rescued. Some fulfilment writers in the Murray-Vos line grant a future large-scale Jewish turning, which narrows the gap between the camps.

promises.title: His feet on the Mount of Olives
promises.promise: Zechariah 14 describes a day of the LORD when the nations gather against Jerusalem, the city is taken and half its people go into exile (14:1-2). Then the LORD fights for his people: his feet stand on the Mount of Olives, which splits from east to west, living waters flow from Jerusalem to east and west (14:8), and the LORD becomes king over all the earth (14:9). The survivors of the nations go up yearly to worship the King and keep the feast of Booths (14:16), and even the bells of the horses bear 'Holy to the LORD' (14:20).

path.text: The LORD will be king over all the earth; on that day the LORD will be one and his name one.
The glory of the LORD left the temple and stood on the mountain east of the city, the Mount of Olives; Zechariah sees the LORD return to the same place.
Jesus ascends from the Mount of Olives (called Olivet), and the angels say he will come in the same way as they saw him go.
On the last great day of the feast of Booths, when water rites recalled the hope of Zechariah 14:8, Jesus offers rivers of living water: the Spirit.
A river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and there is no more curse, which echoes Zechariah 14:8 and 14:11.

promises.history: Zechariah 9-14 is undated and its date is disputed, though many place it in the Persian period after 520 BC. The Mount of Olives lies east of Jerusalem across the Kidron valley. Jesus taught there about Jerusalem's fall (Mark 13:3), wept over the city from its slope (Luke 19:37-41) and ascended from it (Acts 1:12). In the siege of AD 70 Titus stationed the Tenth Legion on the Mount of Olives (Josephus, Jewish War 5.70), and the city was taken and its people killed or exiled, which preterist readers compare with Zechariah 14:1-2.
promises.toUs: Both camps agree the chapter points to the LORD's universal kingship, which believers already confess in Jesus as Lord of all (Acts 10:36). On the fulfilment reading, the living waters already flow through the Spirit (John 7:38) and the universal holiness of 14:20-21 is pictured in the church as God's temple and completed when the whole new Jerusalem is holy. Christians wait with hope for the visible return of the King who left from Olivet.
promises.futurist: Dispensationalists read the chapter literally: at the end of the tribulation the nations besiege Jerusalem, Jesus returns bodily to the Mount of Olives (as Acts 1:11-12 implies), the mountain physically splits, a river flows from Jerusalem to the Dead Sea and the Mediterranean, and Christ reigns from Jerusalem in the millennium. The yearly pilgrimage for Booths, with punishment of drought on nations that refuse (14:17-19), shows a world where sin and death still exist, which fits the millennium and not the eternal state. Writers such as Walvoord and Fruchtenbaum note that a fault line runs through the area.
promises.reply: Fulfilment writers give two main readings. Many amillennialists treat Zechariah 14 as apocalyptic imagery of the final victory of God, using Israel's feasts and geography to picture a renewed world, fulfilled at Christ's return and in the new creation where the river of life flows (Revelation 22:1). Preterists such as Gentry and Chilton see 14:1-2 as the Roman siege of AD 70, followed by the spread of the gospel (living waters to east and west) and the nations worshipping the King. Both note that Acts 1:11 speaks of the manner of his coming (visible, with clouds) rather than a geological event, and that John 7 already links the feast of Booths' water to the Spirit.
promises.rejoinder: Dispensationalists answer that the angels speak at the same mountain, and Luke takes care to name it (Acts 1:12), which strengthens a literal link with Zechariah 14:4. They argue that a siege that ends with God defeating the attackers (14:3, 14:12) cannot describe AD 70, when Rome won, and that the punishment of nations that refuse to keep Booths makes no sense in a sinless new creation. This, they say, requires an intermediate earthly kingdom.

landWidening.label: Eden: the first sanctuary-land
landWidening.text: God places the man in a garden in Eden 'to work it and keep it', the same pair of verbs later used for the priests' service in the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8). Beale and others read Eden as the first temple-land, and Adam was told to fill and subdue the whole earth (Genesis 1:28), so God's dwelling was meant to spread to the ends of the earth. Exile from Eden (Genesis 3:23-24) is the first loss of land, and every later land promise answers it.

landWidening.label: Canaan promised to Abraham
landWidening.text: God promises Abraham's offspring the land from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates, and later gives it as 'an everlasting possession' (Genesis 17:8). The promise is made inside a wider one: all families of the earth will be blessed in Abraham (Genesis 12:3). Yet Abraham himself owned only a burial cave at Machpelah (Genesis 23), a sign that the promise looked beyond his lifetime.

landWidening.label: The land given under Joshua and Solomon
landWidening.text: After the conquest, Joshua records that the LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to their fathers, and 'not one word failed' of all his good promises. Under Solomon, Judah and Israel were as many as the sand of the sea, and Solomon ruled from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt (1 Kings 4:20-21), matching Genesis 15:18 and 22:17. Fulfilment writers stress these texts as evidence that the land promise was kept in history; dispensationalists answer that the borders were not held permanently and that Solomon's rule was over subject kingdoms, so a final possession remains.

landWidening.label: The prophets enlarge the vision
landWidening.text: After exile, Isaiah tells Zion to enlarge the place of her tent, because her offspring will possess the nations and spread to the right and the left. The royal psalms already promised the king 'the nations as your heritage and the ends of the earth as your possession' (Psalms 2:8) and a rule 'from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth' (Psalms 72:8). Here the borders of Canaan start to widen into the whole world, under the Davidic king.

landWidening.label: Heir of the world; the meek inherit the earth
landWidening.text: Paul says the promise to Abraham and his offspring was that he would be 'heir of the world', through the righteousness of faith. Jesus takes Psalms 37:11 ('the meek shall inherit the land') and says 'the meek shall inherit the earth' (Matthew 5:5). Fulfilment writers such as Robertson, Martin and Burge see this as the New Testament's own statement that Canaan was a type of the whole earth; dispensationalists such as Vlach and Horner reply that the whole includes the part, so the widening does not cancel Israel's particular land.

landWidening.label: A better, heavenly country
landWidening.text: Hebrews says the patriarchs died in faith without receiving what was promised, confessing they were strangers and exiles on the earth, seeking a homeland. They desired 'a better country, that is, a heavenly one', and God has prepared a city for them (11:16), the city with foundations whose builder is God (11:10). Even while living in Canaan, Abraham looked beyond it, so the patriarchs themselves read the land promise as pointing higher.

landWidening.label: New heavens and new earth
landWidening.text: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the new Jerusalem coming down from God; the dwelling place of God is with people, and he will dwell with them. The city is a cube (21:16) like the Most Holy Place, so the whole renewed world becomes God's sanctuary, and the river and tree of life return from Eden (22:1-2). Both camps agree the story ends here; they differ on whether an earthly millennial kingdom centred on Israel's land comes first, and on whether the renewed earth keeps a special place for the land of Israel.

modern.intro: Three separate questions are often tangled together when Christians speak about the modern State of Israel, and this section keeps them apart. First, a theological question: is the founding of the state in 1948, and events since, a fulfilment of biblical prophecy? Christians answer this differently, and both answers are set out below with their best arguments. Second, a historical question: how did the state actually come into being? Here the record is largely agreed: a mostly secular national movement (Zionism) born in late nineteenth-century Europe, British imperial decisions (the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate), the catastrophe of the Holocaust, a United Nations vote in 1947, and the outcome of the 1948-49 war, which also displaced some 700,000 Palestinian Arabs. Third, a moral question: the dignity, safety and worth of the Jewish people. That question does not depend on the answer to the first. A Christian may hold that 1948 is not a fulfilment of prophecy and still honour the Jewish people, oppose antisemitism, and affirm the right of every people, Jewish and Palestinian, to live in safety. A Christian may hold that it is a fulfilment and still care for justice for Palestinians, many of whom are Christians. This study takes no side on current political or military disputes.

timeline.label: AD 70: Jerusalem and the temple destroyed
timeline.text: Roman forces under Titus captured Jerusalem in AD 70 after a long siege and burned the second temple. Josephus describes great loss of life and the taking of many captives. Jesus had foretold this judgment in Luke 19:41-44 and Luke 21:20-24. Jewish life continued in Galilee and in the wider diaspora, but the temple and its sacrifices ended.

timeline.label: AD 132-135: Bar Kokhba revolt and Aelia Capitolina
timeline.text: A second Jewish revolt, led by Simon bar Kosiba (called Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star'), was crushed by Hadrian's armies by AD 135. Rabbi Akiva is reported to have hailed Bar Kokhba as the Messiah. Hadrian refounded Jerusalem as a Roman colony, Aelia Capitolina, and Jews were barred from entering the city. The province was renamed Syria Palaestina; whether this was meant as a punishment is disputed among historians.

timeline.label: 1609: Thomas Brightman and the Puritan hope
timeline.text: The English Puritan Thomas Brightman (1562-1607) argued in his commentary on Revelation, Apocalypsis Apocalypseos (published 1609), that the Jews would be converted to Christ and return to their land. This joined two ideas that many later Puritans held together: a future large-scale conversion of the Jews (from Romans 11:25-26) and a future return to the land. Brightman expected the conversion first; for him, return followed faith.

timeline.label: 1655-56: Jews readmitted to England
timeline.text: The Amsterdam rabbi Menasseh ben Israel petitioned Oliver Cromwell to readmit Jews to England, from which they had been expelled in 1290. The Whitehall Conference of December 1655 reached no formal decision, but Jewish residence was tolerated from 1656. Puritan hopes for the conversion of the Jews formed part of the background, alongside trade and religious toleration.

timeline.label: 1669: Increase Mather, The Mystery of Israel's Salvation
timeline.text: The New England minister Increase Mather (1639-1723) published The Mystery of Israel's Salvation Explained and Applyed (London, 1669). He argued that the Jewish people would be converted in large numbers and restored to their land before the end. Like most restorationists of this era, he tied the return to conversion, not to a political project. Iain Murray's The Puritan Hope traces this tradition.

timeline.label: 1831-33: J. N. Darby and the Powerscourt conferences
timeline.text: John Nelson Darby (1800-1882), a leader of the Plymouth Brethren, developed his teaching at prophecy meetings such as the Powerscourt conferences in Ireland (1831-1833). He drew a sharp line between Israel (God's earthly people) and the church (God's heavenly people) and taught a secret rapture of the church before God resumes His dealings with Israel. This system, later called dispensationalism, gave restoration a new shape: Israel could return to the land in unbelief before its national conversion.

timeline.label: 1838-1840s: Lord Shaftesbury and restorationism in Britain
timeline.text: Anthony Ashley-Cooper, later the seventh Earl of Shaftesbury, an evangelical, urged the British government to support Jewish return to Palestine. Britain opened a vice-consulate in Jerusalem in 1838, and in 1840 Shaftesbury pressed Foreign Secretary Palmerston to sponsor Jewish settlement. The slogan 'a land without a people for a people without a land' is often credited to him. Its attribution is contested: similar wording appears in the Scottish minister Alexander Keith (1843) and in Shaftesbury's later writings, and Israel Zangwill popularised it around 1901. The phrase is also disputed in substance, since the land had a settled Arab population.

timeline.label: 1881-82: Russian pogroms and the First Aliyah
timeline.text: After the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in March 1881, waves of anti-Jewish riots (pogroms) swept the south-western Russian Empire. The restrictive 'May Laws' of 1882 followed. Most Jews who left went to the United States, but small groups such as Bilu and Hovevei Zion (Lovers of Zion) began the First Aliyah (1882-1903), founding farming settlements such as Rishon LeZion (1882). Their motive was mainly safety and national renewal, not the fulfilment of prophecy.

timeline.label: 1891: The Blackstone Memorial
timeline.text: William E. Blackstone, a Chicago businessman and author of the premillennial bestseller Jesus Is Coming (1878), presented a petition to President Benjamin Harrison in March 1891. It asked the United States to support giving Palestine back to the Jews and was signed by over 400 prominent Americans, including business leaders, editors and clergy. No action followed, but the Memorial is often cited as an early landmark of American Christian Zionism.

timeline.label: 1896: Theodor Herzl, Der Judenstaat
timeline.text: The Viennese journalist Theodor Herzl (1860-1904) published Der Judenstaat ('The Jewish State') in February 1896. He argued that antisemitism would not disappear in Europe and that Jews needed a state of their own, secured by international agreement. His case was political and largely secular; he even considered places other than Palestine. The Dreyfus affair in France (from 1894) is often linked to his thinking, though how much it shaped him is disputed.

timeline.label: 1897: First Zionist Congress, Basel
timeline.text: Herzl convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel, Switzerland, on 29-31 August 1897. It founded the Zionist Organization and adopted the Basel Program, which aimed to create for the Jewish people a home in Palestine 'secured by public law'. Most delegates were secular or traditional rather than strictly Orthodox, and many leading Orthodox rabbis opposed the movement at this time.

timeline.label: 1909: The Scofield Reference Bible
timeline.text: Oxford University Press published the Scofield Reference Bible, edited by C. I. Scofield, in 1909 (revised 1917). Its notes spread Darby's dispensational scheme, including a future national restoration of Israel, among millions of English-speaking Protestants. Many readers met the Israel-church distinction in the margin of their Bibles rather than in theology books.

timeline.label: 1917: The Balfour Declaration
timeline.text: On 2 November 1917, Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour wrote to Lord Rothschild that the British government viewed with favour 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine. The same letter said nothing should be done to prejudice the civil and religious rights of the existing non-Jewish communities. British motives included wartime strategy, imperial interests near the Suez Canal, and the hope of Jewish support for the Allies; some cabinet members also held restorationist sympathies. In December 1917 General Allenby's forces entered Jerusalem, ending Ottoman rule there.

timeline.label: 1920-22: The British Mandate for Palestine
timeline.text: The San Remo conference (April 1920) assigned Palestine to Britain, and the League of Nations approved the Mandate in July 1922; it took effect in 1923. The Mandate text included the Balfour Declaration's commitment to a Jewish national home. In the same period Britain separated Transjordan from the area open to Jewish settlement. Jewish immigration and land purchase grew, and so did Arab opposition, with serious violence in 1920, 1921 and 1929.

timeline.label: 1933-45: The Holocaust
timeline.text: From the Nazi seizure of power in 1933, Jews in Germany faced growing persecution, and during the Second World War some six million Jews were murdered in a deliberate programme of genocide. Many survivors had no homes to return to, and many were held in displaced persons camps after 1945. The Holocaust convinced much of the world, and most Jews, that a Jewish state was a necessity for safety.

timeline.label: 1937: The Peel Commission proposes partition
timeline.text: After the Arab revolt began in 1936, a British Royal Commission led by Lord Peel reported in July 1937 that the Mandate was unworkable. It proposed dividing the land into a small Jewish state and an Arab state joined to Transjordan, with a British zone around Jerusalem. The Zionist leadership was divided but open to negotiation; the Arab Higher Committee rejected it. The plan was later dropped.

timeline.label: 1939: The British White Paper
timeline.text: In May 1939 the British government issued a White Paper limiting Jewish immigration to 75,000 over five years, restricting land sales, and proposing an independent Palestine within ten years. It aimed to secure Arab goodwill as war with Germany approached. Zionists saw it as a betrayal, coming just as European Jews most needed refuge.

timeline.label: 1947: UN Partition Plan (Resolution 181)
timeline.text: On 29 November 1947 the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 181 by 33 votes to 13, with 10 abstentions. It recommended ending the Mandate and dividing the land into a Jewish state and an Arab state, with Jerusalem under an international regime. The Jewish Agency accepted the plan; the Arab Higher Committee and the Arab states rejected it. Fighting between Jewish and Arab communities broke out almost at once.

timeline.label: 14 May 1948: The State of Israel is declared
timeline.text: On 14 May 1948, the day before the Mandate ended, David Ben-Gurion read the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel in Tel Aviv. The text grounds the state in Jewish history, the Balfour Declaration, the Holocaust and the UN resolution. It speaks of trust in the 'Rock of Israel', a phrase chosen so that both religious and secular signers could accept it. The United States recognised the state within minutes (de facto), and the Soviet Union gave full legal recognition three days later.

timeline.label: 1948-49: The war and Palestinian displacement
timeline.text: Armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered the conflict on 15 May 1948. By the 1949 armistice agreements Israel held more territory than the partition plan had assigned; Egypt held Gaza and Transjordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem. About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled from their homes and were not allowed to return; Palestinians call this the Nakba ('catastrophe'). The causes and the balance of flight and expulsion are debated by historians. In the following decades a comparable number of Jews left or were driven from Arab and Muslim countries, many settling in Israel.

timeline.label: 1950: The Law of Return
timeline.text: On 5 July 1950 Israel's parliament (the Knesset) passed the Law of Return, giving every Jew the right to settle in Israel as a citizen. A 1970 amendment extended this to children and grandchildren of Jews and their spouses. The law defines the state's purpose as a refuge for Jews; it is a civil law, not a religious decree, and the question 'who is a Jew' under it has been debated in Israel ever since.

timeline.label: 1967: The Six-Day War and East Jerusalem
timeline.text: In the war of 5-10 June 1967, Israel took Sinai and Gaza from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria. Israeli troops reached the Western Wall on 7 June. Israel later applied its law to East Jerusalem; most states and the UN have not recognised this annexation. For many evangelical prophecy writers this event was decisive: L. Nelson Bell wrote in Christianity Today (July 1967) that Jerusalem being wholly in Jewish hands for the first time in over 2,000 years gave new confidence in the Bible, and Luke 21:24 became a central proof-text.

timeline.label: 1970: Hal Lindsey, The Late Great Planet Earth
timeline.text: Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (Zondervan, 1970), written with C. C. Carlson, became one of the best-selling non-fiction books in the United States in the 1970s. It read 1948 as the budding of the fig tree (Matthew 24:32-34) and suggested that the end-time events would come within about forty years, one generation, of 1948. It also identified Russia with Gog of Ezekiel 38. The book brought dispensational prophecy about Israel into popular culture.

timeline.label: 1973: The Yom Kippur War
timeline.text: On 6 October 1973, the Day of Atonement, Egypt and Syria attacked Israeli positions in Sinai and the Golan Heights. After heavy losses and early setbacks, Israel regained the initiative; a ceasefire came later that month. Arab oil producers imposed an oil embargo on states that backed Israel. Prophecy writing responded quickly, for example John Walvoord's Armageddon, Oil and the Middle East Crisis (1974).

timeline.label: 1980: International Christian Embassy Jerusalem
timeline.text: In 1980 Israel's Knesset passed the Jerusalem Law, and the UN Security Council (Resolution 478) called on states to withdraw their embassies from the city; thirteen states moved their embassies to Tel Aviv.
