readings.reading: Ethnic Israel will turn to Christ in large numbers at or just before his return, when they see him (Matthew 23:39; Zechariah 12:10). They will enter the one people of God, not a separate program, and share in Christ's millennial reign on earth with the church.
readings.holders: George Eldon Ladd (A Theology of the New Testament, 1974; The Presence of the Future), Craig Blomberg, Barry Horner (a more national view), and many earlier premillennialists such as J. C. Ryle.
readings.strengths: It joins the strengths of the future-conversion reading with a straightforward reading of Revelation 20. It ties Jesus' words 'you will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes' (Matthew 23:39) to Israel's future welcome of the Messiah. It avoids a strict two-peoples theology.
readings.weaknesses: Amillennialists answer that Romans 11 gives no hint of a millennium after this conversion; Paul moves straight to doxology (Romans 11:33-36). Dispensationalists, on the other side, say it is inconsistent to read Romans 11 ethnically while reading the land promises typologically.

hermeneutics.title: Which Testament has the last word?
hermeneutics.fulfilment: The fulfilment family holds that the New Testament gives the final and authoritative sense of Old Testament promises. Jesus explained 'in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself' (Luke 24:27), and Peter says the prophets searched for the time of Christ's sufferings and glories (1 Peter 1:10-12). Later revelation does not contradict earlier promises, but it can show that they are fulfilled more fully than first readers could see.
hermeneutics.future: The future family answers that the Old Testament must be read on its own terms first, because its first hearers were meant to understand it. Robert Saucy and Michael Vlach argue that the New Testament adds to Old Testament promises (for example, including Gentiles) but does not cancel or redefine what God promised to Israel. Otherwise, they say, the original promises would have misled their hearers.

hermeneutics.title: Literal or typological fulfilment
hermeneutics.fulfilment: Fulfilment scholars insist they read literally in the sense of 'as the author meant', but that the Bible itself uses types: Adam, David, the temple and the land point beyond themselves (Romans 5:14; Colossians 2:17). A type is a real thing in history that also foreshadows a greater reality. When the reality comes, the shadow is not restored but surpassed.
hermeneutics.future: Dispensationalists such as Charles Ryrie call for consistent 'plain' or 'normal' interpretation of prophecy. They accept types, but deny that types cancel the original reference. Progressive dispensationalists speak of 'complementary' fulfilment: the church may share in a promise without removing its fulfilment for Israel.

hermeneutics.title: The 'seed' of Abraham
hermeneutics.fulfilment: Paul's argument in Galatians 3:16 that the promise was made to Abraham's 'seed', singular, that is, Christ, is decisive for the fulfilment reading. The promises narrow to one Israelite, then widen to everyone in him: 'if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's seed' (Galatians 3:29). Physical descent alone never guaranteed the promise (Romans 9:6-8).
hermeneutics.future: The future family accepts that Christ is the ultimate seed and that believers share in Abraham's blessing. But they note that 'seed' in Genesis also means the physical nation (Genesis 15:13; Genesis 17:7-8), and that Paul still calls unbelieving Jews 'my kinsmen according to the flesh' to whom 'the promises' belong (Romans 9:3-4). Several senses of 'seed' work together; one does not erase another.

hermeneutics.title: Conditional or unconditional covenants
hermeneutics.fulfilment: Fulfilment scholars note that life in the land was tied to obedience: Israel would be uprooted for unfaithfulness (Deuteronomy 28:63-64), and Joshua says that God kept every land promise (Joshua 21:43-45). The unconditional element of the covenant is God's commitment to bring his promise to pass, which he did in Christ, the obedient Israelite who kept the conditions for his people.
hermeneutics.future: Dispensationalists distinguish the Abrahamic covenant, unconditional and ratified by God alone passing between the pieces (Genesis 15:17-18), from the Mosaic covenant, which governed Israel's enjoyment of the land in any one generation. Even in exile God promised not to break his covenant (Leviticus 26:44-45). Joshua 21:43-45 describes a stage, not the final possession, since later texts still promise the land (Amos 9:14-15).

hermeneutics.title: What 'forever' means
hermeneutics.fulfilment: The Hebrew word often rendered 'forever' ('olam) means a long or unlimited age within a given order. The Passover was a statute 'forever' (Exodus 12:14) and Phinehas received a 'perpetual priesthood' (Numbers 25:13), yet Hebrews says the priesthood and law have been changed (Hebrews 7:12). Fulfilment scholars say the 'everlasting' land promise is kept forever in the everlasting inheritance of the new earth.
hermeneutics.future: The future family answers that when God swears 'forever' about the land and the nation, he means it, and backs it with oaths tied to the sun and moon (Jeremiah 31:35-37). Changes in the priesthood are explained in Scripture itself; no text explains a change to the land promise. To spiritualise 'forever' for the land, they argue, weakens the sure promises given to the church as well.

hermeneutics.title: Israel and the church: one people or two?
hermeneutics.fulfilment: The fulfilment family holds that there is one people of God across both Testaments, one olive tree with one root (Romans 11:17-24). Christ has broken down the dividing wall and made Jew and Gentile one new man (Ephesians 2:14-16). Gentile believers are no longer strangers to 'the commonwealth of Israel' (Ephesians 2:12, 19). This is not 'replacement' but enlargement and fulfilment.
hermeneutics.future: Classic dispensationalists hold that Israel and the church are distinct peoples with distinct destinies. Paul still distinguishes 'Jews, Greeks and the church of God' (1 Corinthians 10:32). Progressive dispensationalists soften the distinction: the church is one people now, but within it Israel remains a nation with future promises, just as Gentile nations remain nations.

hermeneutics.title: Acts 15 and the fallen tent of David
hermeneutics.fulfilment: At the Jerusalem council James cites Amos 9:11-12 to show that the inclusion of Gentiles agrees with the prophets (Acts 15:15-17). Fulfilment scholars read this as proof that the 'rebuilding of David's fallen tent' is happening now, through the risen Son of David gathering Jews and Gentiles. The Davidic restoration is not postponed.
hermeneutics.future: Dispensationalists read James as saying the Gentile mission agrees with the prophets, not that it fulfils the whole of Amos 9. Walvoord placed the rebuilding 'after this' (Acts 15:16) at Christ's return. Progressive dispensationalists accept an inaugurated fulfilment now but point to Amos 9:14-15, which promises Israel will be planted in its land and never uprooted, as still awaiting completion.

hermeneutics.title: Hebrews: shadows and substance
hermeneutics.fulfilment: Hebrews calls the law 'a shadow of the good things to come' (Hebrews 10:1), the earthly tabernacle a copy (Hebrews 8:5), and the first covenant 'obsolete and growing old' (Hebrews 8:13). It also says that Abraham sought a better, heavenly country (Hebrews 11:16). For the fulfilment family, this rules out a return to animal sacrifices or a rebuilt temple, which would turn back from substance to shadow.
hermeneutics.future: Dispensationalists accept that sacrifices cannot take away sin. Those who expect a millennial temple (Ezekiel 40-48) usually read its sacrifices as memorials of Christ's death or as ceremonial cleansing for God's presence among mortals, a view defended by Jerry Hullinger. Others read Ezekiel's sacrifices in the prophet's own terms of reference. They argue Hebrews addresses the Levitical system as a means of approach to God, not every future use of a temple.

exchanges.title: Galatians 3:16 and 3:29: the promises were spoken to one Seed
exchanges.argument: Paul stresses that God's promises were spoken to Abraham and to his 'seed', singular, not to many seeds, and he names that Seed as Christ (Galatians 3:16). He then concludes that all who belong to Christ, Jew or Gentile, are Abraham's seed and heirs by promise (Galatians 3:29). On this reading the promises were never addressed to a bloodline as such but to the Messiah and to those united to him. Robertson and Hoekema argue that this is Paul's own key to every promise made to Abraham, including the land.
exchanges.counter: Dispensationalists reply that Paul's point in Galatians 3 is about how a person is justified, not about who owns the land or the national promises. Genesis 13:15 and 17:8 also speak of a collective offspring who receive Canaan, and Paul himself still speaks of Israel according to the flesh as a people with a future (Romans 11:1, 11:28). Vlach argues that Gentiles share in Abraham's spiritual blessings without becoming Israel or absorbing Israel's national promises.
exchanges.answer: Fulfilment writers answer that Paul does not limit his argument to justification: he speaks of 'the inheritance' (Galatians 3:18) and of 'heirs according to the promise' (Galatians 3:29), and the inheritance in Genesis is the land. They also note that Paul widens that inheritance to 'the world' in Romans 4:13. If the heirs are those in Christ and the inheritance is the world, no separate ethnic inheritance is left over.

exchanges.title: Romans 2:28-29 and 9:6-8: not all who are from Israel are Israel
exchanges.argument: Paul says a person is not a Jew merely outwardly, nor is circumcision merely in the flesh; the true Jew is one inwardly, with circumcision of the heart by the Spirit (Romans 2:28-29). In Romans 9:6-8 he explains that God's word has not failed, because not all who descend from Israel are Israel, and the children of the promise are counted as the seed. The fulfilment reading holds that 'Israel' in God's purpose was always defined by promise and faith, not by birth alone. Gentiles who believe are grafted into this one olive tree (Romans 11:17).
exchanges.counter: Future-for-Israel scholars agree that Romans 9:6 distinguishes a believing remnant within Israel, but they stress that it is a remnant within ethnic Israel, not Gentiles. The 'Israel' of 9:6 is still Jewish; Paul is narrowing, not widening. Moo, who is not a dispensationalist, also reads 9:6 this way. So the verse supports a true Israel inside Israel, not a church that is Israel.
exchanges.answer: Fulfilment writers grant that 9:6 narrows Israel to the remnant, but they point out that Paul immediately widens the called people to include Gentiles, quoting Hosea's 'not my people' who become 'my people' (Romans 9:24-26). The principle that sonship is by promise, not flesh, is what lets Gentiles join the one tree. Romans 2:28-29 also defines the Jew by the Spirit, and Philippians 3:3 applies 'the circumcision' to a mixed church.

exchanges.title: Ephesians 2:11-22: one new man, the dividing wall gone
exchanges.argument: Paul tells Gentile believers that they were once strangers to the commonwealth of Israel and to the covenants of promise (Ephesians 2:12). In Christ the dividing wall has been broken down and the two have been made into 'one new man' (Ephesians 2:14-15). Gentiles are now fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household, a holy temple built on the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:19-22). Fulfilment writers argue that a future arrangement in which Israel again stands apart from Gentile believers, with its own temple and privileges, would rebuild the very wall Christ destroyed.
exchanges.counter: Progressive dispensationalists, such as Saucy and Blaising and Bock, agree that Jew and Gentile are one in Christ in the church. They argue that unity does not erase distinctions, just as male and female remain distinct while being one in Christ (Galatians 3:28). Nations remain nations in the new creation (Revelation 21:24), so Israel can remain a nation among nations without any wall of hostility.
exchanges.answer: Fulfilment writers answer that Ephesians 2 does not only remove hostility; it brings Gentiles into the commonwealth and covenants once belonging to Israel. Gentiles do not get a lesser share, they are 'fellow heirs' (Ephesians 3:6). A future in which ethnic Israel holds land, temple or priestly rank that believing Gentiles do not share would, in their view, reverse Ephesians 3:6.

exchanges.title: Galatians 6:16: 'the Israel of God'
exchanges.argument: Galatians closes with a blessing on all who walk by the rule that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but a new creation (Galatians 6:15-16). Paul calls this group 'the Israel of God'. In a letter written to stop Gentiles being made to live as Jews, the fulfilment reading holds that Paul names the whole church, Jew and Gentile, as God's Israel. Calvin, Robertson and many others read the 'and' as explanatory: peace on them, that is, on the Israel of God.
exchanges.counter: Many future-for-Israel scholars, following S. Lewis Johnson and others, hold that the 'and' is additive: Paul blesses the Gentile believers who walk by this rule 'and also' the believing Jews, the Israel of God. They note that nowhere else does the New Testament plainly call the church 'Israel'. On this view the phrase refers to Jewish Christians, a remnant inside Israel.
exchanges.answer: Fulfilment writers reply that singling out Jewish believers at the climax of a letter that has just said circumcision counts for nothing would undercut Paul's whole argument. Even if 'Israel of God' meant Jewish believers only, it still defines Israel by faith in Christ, not by birth. And the idea that believers are Israel does not rest on this verse alone, but also on Romans 2:29, Philippians 3:3 and 1 Peter 2:9.

exchanges.title: 1 Peter 2:9-10: the titles of Exodus 19 given to the church
exchanges.argument: At Sinai God called Israel his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exodus 19:5-6). Peter gives these same titles to scattered believers: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession (1 Peter 2:9). He adds Hosea's words: once not a people, now God's people (1 Peter 2:10; Hosea 2:23). The fulfilment reading holds that Peter transfers Israel's covenant identity, without remainder, to the church built on the living Stone, Christ (1 Peter 2:4-8).
exchanges.counter: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that 1 Peter may be addressed mainly to Jewish believers of the dispersion (1 Peter 1:1 uses 'diaspora'), so Peter may be describing the believing remnant of Israel. Even if Gentiles are included, sharing titles shows likeness, not identity. Israel was called to be a light to nations; the church shares that calling without cancelling Israel's national future.
exchanges.answer: Fulfilment writers note that Peter says his readers once lived in ignorance and in the 'futile ways inherited from your forefathers' (1 Peter 1:14, 1:18) and that they were once 'not a people' (1 Peter 2:10), which fits Gentiles better than Jews. Every title Exodus 19 gave Israel is here given to the church; it is hard to name an identity of Israel at Sinai that Peter withholds.

exchanges.title: Hebrews 8-10: shadows made obsolete; a rebuilt temple would be a step back
exchanges.argument: Hebrews quotes the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31-34 and concludes that by calling it 'new', God has made the first one old, and what is growing old is near to vanishing (Hebrews 8:13). The law had only a shadow of the good things to come (Hebrews 10:1), and Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time (Hebrews 10:12-14). On this reading, a future temple with animal sacrifices, as many dispensationalists expect from Ezekiel 40-48, would return to the shadow after the reality has come. Beale argues that the temple was always meant to expand into Christ and his people (John 2:19-21; 1 Corinthians 3:16).
exchanges.counter: Dispensationalists answer that millennial sacrifices would not take away sin. Some (Whitcomb, Hullinger) say they would be memorials, like the Lord's Supper, or would deal with ceremonial uncleanness caused by God's presence among mortal people. Ezekiel 40-48 gives detailed measures and rules that, in their view, cannot easily be read as symbols, and Ezekiel 43:10-11 tells Israel to keep its whole design.
exchanges.answer: Fulfilment writers reply that Hebrews says the old system was set aside 'because of its weakness and uselessness' (Hebrews 7:18) and that where there is forgiveness there is no longer any offering for sin (Hebrews 10:18). They argue that Ezekiel described the coming restoration in the only temple terms his hearers knew, and that Revelation 21:22 says the new Jerusalem has no temple, for the Lord and the Lamb are its temple.

exchanges.title: 2 Corinthians 1:20: all God's promises are 'Yes' in Christ
exchanges.argument: Paul says that however many God's promises are, in Christ they are 'Yes', and through him we say 'Amen' to God's glory (2 Corinthians 1:20). The fulfilment reading treats this as a rule for reading the Old Testament: every promise finds its fulfilment in Christ. This does not empty the promises but makes them larger, as when David's throne becomes Christ's throne at God's right hand (Acts 2:30-36). Gentry and Wellum argue that the covenants form one story that reaches its goal in Jesus.
exchanges.counter: Future-for-Israel scholars agree that every promise is confirmed in Christ, but they say 'Yes in Christ' means guaranteed by him, not reinterpreted by him. Romans 15:8 says Christ became a servant to the circumcision to confirm the promises given to the fathers. A promise of land to Israel confirmed by Christ will be kept to Israel when Christ returns.
exchanges.answer: Fulfilment writers answer that Romans 15:8-12 goes straight on to show Gentiles glorifying God, so the confirmed promises already include the nations. They also argue that 'confirmed in Christ' must include how Christ fulfils them, which the New Testament shows: the temple in his body, the throne at God's right hand, the land widened to the world. The question is not whether the promises stand but what shape their fulfilment takes.

exchanges.title: Matthew 21:43: the kingdom given to a nation producing its fruits
exchanges.argument: After the parable of the wicked tenants, Jesus tells the chief priests and elders that the kingdom of God will be taken from them and given to a nation producing its fruits (Matthew 21:43). The fulfilment reading holds that this new 'nation' is the community of Jesus' followers, Jew and Gentile, echoing 1 Peter 2:9, 'a holy nation'. Holwerda and France argue that Jesus here redefines the people of the kingdom around himself as the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone (Matthew 21:42).
exchanges.counter: Dispensationalists answer that the kingdom was taken from that generation of leaders, not from Israel forever. Jesus is speaking to the chief priests and Pharisees (Matthew 21:45), and the 'nation' may be a future generation of Israel that will repent and say 'Blessed is he who comes' (Matthew 23:39). Vlach and other dispensational writers read it this way.
exchanges.answer: Fulfilment writers reply that the vineyard image comes from Isaiah 5, where the vineyard is the whole house of Israel, and the tenants' judgment fell on the whole city in AD 70 (Matthew 22:7). They grant that individual Jews remain welcome; the point is that the kingdom's people are now defined by fruit and by the cornerstone, not by ancestry.

exchanges.title: Hebrews 11:10-16 and the silence on land: the patriarchs sought a better country
exchanges.argument: Hebrews says Abraham lived in the promised land as a foreigner, because he was looking for the city whose builder is God (Hebrews 11:9-10). The patriarchs desired a better, heavenly country, so God has prepared a city for them (Hebrews 11:16). Davies and Burge note that the New Testament never repeats a promise of the land of Canaan to ethnic Israel; instead Abraham is 'heir of the world' (Romans 4:13) and the meek inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5, from Psalms 37:11). The fulfilment reading holds that the land was a down payment on the renewed creation.
exchanges.counter: Future-for-Israel scholars answer that silence is not cancellation: the land promise was everlasting and unconditional and needed no repeating. They point to hints that do appear: Jesus' saying that Jerusalem will be trampled 'until' the times of the Gentiles end (Luke 21:24), the disciples' question in Acts 1:6, and Paul's present-tense list of Israel's privileges (Romans 9:4). They add that the 'heavenly country' comes down to earth (Revelation 21:2) and can include the land of Israel.
exchanges.answer: Fulfilment writers reply that they also expect a renewed, physical earth, and that the land of Israel will certainly be part of it, but as part of a world given to all the meek, not as an ethnic territory. If the New Testament writers believed in a coming national restoration in the land, it is striking that they never say so plainly in a letter about Israel's future such as Romans 9-11.

exchanges.title: AD 70 as the judgment that ended the old covenant age
exchanges.argument: Jesus wept over Jerusalem and said its house would be left desolate (Matthew 23:37-38). He foretold that no stone of the temple would stand on another (Matthew 24:2) and that the city would be surrounded by armies and its people led captive among the nations (Luke 21:20-24). This happened in AD 70, when Titus's army destroyed the temple, as Josephus records. Fulfilment writers, especially preterists and postmillennialists, hold that AD 70 marked the end of the old covenant age, so that God's people are no longer centred on one city and temple (John 4:21-24).
exchanges.counter: Future-for-Israel scholars agree that AD 70 was a judgment, but they note that Luke 21:24 sets a limit: Jerusalem will be trampled 'until' the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. Judgment in the Old Testament was always followed by promised restoration (Deuteronomy 30:1-5; Jeremiah 30:11). AD 70 repeats the pattern of 586 BC, after which God brought the people back.
exchanges.answer: Fulfilment writers answer that the restoration after exile in the Old Testament was itself a pointer to the greater restoration in Christ, who gathers the scattered children of God into one (John 11:51-52). 'Until' in Luke 21:24 sets a time limit on Gentile rule over the city, but it does not say what follows; many read it as the end of the age at Christ's return rather than a national restoration.

exchanges.title: Romans 11:1-2: 'Has God rejected his people? By no means'
exchanges.argument: Paul asks directly whether God has rejected his people, and answers no: he himself is an Israelite, of Abraham's seed, of the tribe of Benjamin (Romans 11:1-2). He then says Israel's stumbling is not a fall beyond recovery, and if their failure means riches for the world, 'how much more' their full inclusion (Romans 11:11-12). Future-for-Israel scholars argue that 'his people' here is ethnic Israel, the very people Paul grieves over in Romans 9:1-5. A view in which Israel's identity passes to the church cannot easily explain why Paul writes three chapters about Israel's future.
exchanges.counter: Fulfilment writers agree that God has not rejected ethnic Jews. Paul's proof is the believing remnant, chosen by grace, of whom he is one (Romans 11:5). Many amillennialists hold that God will keep saving Jews through history; some, such as Murray and Vos, even expect a large future turning. None of this requires a national kingdom or land restoration.
exchanges.answer: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that 'how much more their fullness' (Romans 11:12) and 'life from the dead' (Romans 11:15) point to a future event far bigger than a steady trickle of Jewish converts. If some Reformed scholars concede a future mass conversion, the question becomes why the Old Testament promises tied to Israel's conversion, such as return to the land in Ezekiel 36:24-28, would not come with it.

exchanges.title: Romans 11:26-29: 'all Israel will be saved', the gifts are irrevocable
exchanges.argument: Paul says a partial hardening has come on Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved, as Isaiah promised a Deliverer from Zion (Romans 11:25-26). He adds that as regards the gospel they are enemies for the Gentiles' sake, but as regards election they are beloved for the fathers' sake, for the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:28-29). Future-for-Israel scholars argue that the 'they' who are now enemies and the 'they' who are beloved are the same ethnic group. God's calling of that people cannot be withdrawn.
exchanges.counter: Fulfilment writers are divided here. Some (Calvin, Wright, Robertson) read 'all Israel' as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, or as all elect Jews through history. Others (Murray, Vos, Hodge) accept a future large-scale turning of ethnic Jews to Christ. Both groups note that Paul describes salvation through the Deliverer's new covenant forgiveness (Romans 11:27), not a restored national state or temple.
exchanges.answer: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that once a future mass conversion of ethnic Israel is granted, Romans 11:26 is quoting Isaiah 59:20-21 and Jeremiah 31:33-34, prophecies set within Israel's national restoration. The irrevocable 'gifts' include the covenants and promises listed in Romans 9:4, which Horner and Vlach argue must include the land.

exchanges.title: Jeremiah 31:35-37: Israel as enduring as the sun and moon
exchanges.argument: Directly after the new covenant promise, God says that only if the fixed order of sun, moon and stars departs will the offspring of Israel cease to be a nation before him (Jeremiah 31:35-36). Only if the heavens can be measured will he cast off all Israel's offspring (Jeremiah 31:37). Future-for-Israel scholars argue that God here ties the new covenant to the lasting existence of Israel as a nation. The sun still rises, so Israel remains a nation before God.
exchanges.counter: Fulfilment writers answer that the new covenant in the same chapter is applied in Hebrews 8:8-12 to the church, so the 'Israel' that endures is the people of the new covenant. They also note that God has kept the promise: a remnant of Israel has always believed, and Jewish believers stand at the root of the church (Romans 11:5).
exchanges.answer: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that the text says 'nation' (goy), a word for a political people, and 'offspring', a word for descent. A believing remnant scattered among the nations hardly meets the promise of Israel continuing 'as a nation'. They add that the survival of the Jewish people through two thousand years of exile is itself a sign that God keeps this word.

exchanges.title: Genesis 15: God alone passed between the pieces
exchanges.argument: In Genesis 15 Abram cut animals in two, and a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch, signs of God's presence, passed between the pieces while Abram slept (Genesis 15:12, 17). On that day God made a covenant to give Abram's offspring the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates (Genesis 15:18). Ancient covenants of this kind put the one who passed through under oath. Walvoord, Pentecost and Fruchtenbaum argue that only God took the oath, so the land promise depends on God alone and cannot be lost by Israel's sin; later passages call it an everlasting covenant and possession (Genesis 17:7-8; Psalms 105:8-11).
exchanges.counter: Fulfilment writers agree the covenant is founded on grace, but they note that obedience is still required of the heirs (Genesis 17:9-14; Genesis 18:19) and that the land could be lost by unfaithfulness (Leviticus 26:32-33; Deuteronomy 28:63-64). They also argue that the 'offspring' who receives it is finally Christ (Galatians 3:16), so the unconditional promise is kept unconditionally in him and in those who belong to him.
exchanges.answer: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that disobedience could make a particular generation lose the enjoyment of the land, but never cancel the promise itself. Leviticus 26:42-45 says that even in exile God will remember his covenant with Abraham and the land, and will not reject them. Enjoyment is conditional; ownership is not.

exchanges.title: The language of 'everlasting' and 'never again'
exchanges.argument: God gives Canaan to Abraham's offspring as an 'everlasting possession' (Genesis 17:8), promises David's house a throne established forever (2 Samuel 7:16), and says through Amos that he will plant Israel on its land and they will never again be uprooted (Amos 9:15). Ezekiel promises that Israel will dwell in the land given to Jacob, they and their children's children forever (Ezekiel 37:25). Future-for-Israel scholars argue that such strong, repeated time words cannot mean something temporary or merely symbolic. Kaiser treats the land promise as an enduring strand of the one promise-plan.
exchanges.counter: Fulfilment writers answer that the Hebrew 'olam' can mean 'lasting for the whole of an age or arrangement'; it is used for the Aaronic priesthood (Exodus 40:15), the Passover (Exodus 12:14) and circumcision (Genesis 17:13), all of which the New Testament treats as fulfilled in Christ. The everlasting quality, they say, is kept in Christ: David's throne is everlasting because Jesus reigns forever.
exchanges.answer: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that the priesthood and feasts were explicitly said to be changed in the New Testament (Hebrews 7:12), but no New Testament text says the land promise was changed. Where Scripture is silent, the plain meaning of 'everlasting' should stand. They also note that Amos 9:15 says 'never again', which a period of possession followed by AD 70 does not satisfy.

exchanges.title: Acts 1:6: 'Will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?'
exchanges.argument: After forty days of teaching about the kingdom of God (Acts 1:3), the disciples ask the risen Jesus whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6). Jesus does not correct the content of the question; he says it is not for them to know the times or seasons (Acts 1:7). Future-for-Israel scholars, including Saucy and Bock, argue that if the hope of a restored kingdom to Israel were mistaken, this was the moment to say so. Peter later speaks of 'times of restoration of all things' spoken by the prophets (Acts 3:21).
exchanges.counter: Fulfilment writers answer that Jesus redirects the question: instead of a kingdom in Israel, the disciples will receive the Spirit and witness to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The restoration begins at Pentecost, where Jews from every nation gather (Acts 2:5) and Peter announces that David's heir now sits on his throne at God's right hand (Acts 2:30-36). James sees the rebuilding of David's fallen tent in Gentile conversion (Acts 15:16-17).
exchanges.answer: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that Acts 1:8 tells the disciples what to do in the meantime, but does not deny a future restoration; 'times or seasons' implies there will be such a time. Progressive dispensationalists accept that David's throne is already occupied by Christ at God's right hand, but argue that the 'restoration of all things' in Acts 3:19-21 is linked to Israel's repentance and Christ's return.

exchanges.title: Romans 9:4-5: the covenants and promises are still theirs
exchanges.argument: Paul writes of his kinsmen according to the flesh that they are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship and the promises; to them belong the patriarchs, and from them is the Christ (Romans 9:4-5). Paul uses the present tense ('they are Israelites') of Jews who did not believe in Jesus. Future-for-Israel scholars argue that the covenants and promises still belong to ethnic Israel, even in unbelief. Vlach and Horner hold that this list rules out the idea that the promises have simply passed to the church.
exchanges.counter: Fulfilment writers answer that Paul is listing Israel's historic privileges to show why their unbelief is so tragic, not to say they can inherit apart from Christ. The same chapter says not all from Israel are Israel (Romans 9:6), and Ephesians 2:12 says Gentiles have now been brought into those same 'covenants of promise'. The promises belong to Israel in the sense that they came through Israel and are offered to Israel first (Romans 1:16).
exchanges.answer: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that 'offered first' is not the same as 'belong to'. Paul could have used a past tense and did not. Together with Romans 11:28-29, they argue, the present tense shows that the promises remain addressed to ethnic Israel, even while most of Israel does not yet believe.

exchanges.title: A consistent literal reading: the first advent prophecies came true literally
exchanges.argument: Ryrie names consistent 'normal' or 'plain' interpretation as part of the essence of dispensationalism. Its defenders point out that prophecies of Christ's first coming were fulfilled in plain, physical ways: born in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:5-6), riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:4-5), pierced (Zechariah 12:10; John 19:37). If those were literal, they argue, the promises of Israel's return to the land and Messiah's reign from Jerusalem should be expected to come true literally too. Spiritualising some promises and not others, they say, makes interpretation arbitrary.
exchanges.counter: Fulfilment writers answer that they also read Scripture literally in the sense of 'according to its literary kind', but that the New Testament itself shows prophecy being fulfilled in ways larger than the letter: the temple in Christ's body (John 2:19-21), David's tent in Gentile conversion (Acts 15:16-17), Hosea 11:1 in the child Jesus (Matthew 2:15). Poythress argues that the prophets used the language of their own time to describe a reality that would surpass it.
exchanges.answer: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that the New Testament examples can be read as additional applications that do not cancel the original meaning. Progressive dispensationalists such as Blaising and Bock accept 'complementary' fulfilment: the New Testament adds Gentiles and spiritual depth, but does not take away what was promised to Israel. Both and, not either or.

exchanges.title: Luke 21:24 and Matthew 23:39: the word 'until'
exchanges.argument: Jesus says Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (Luke 21:24). He tells Jerusalem that it will not see him again until it says 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' (Matthew 23:39). Paul says the hardening on Israel lasts until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in (Romans 11:25). Future-for-Israel scholars argue that each 'until' implies a reversal: the Gentile trampling ends, Jerusalem welcomes its Messiah, the hardening lifts.
exchanges.counter: Fulfilment writers answer that 'until' marks a limit but does not always imply a reversal in the same terms (compare 2 Samuel 6:23, where Michal had no child 'until' her death). Matthew 23:39 may mean that Jerusalem will see Jesus only when it is forced to acknowledge him at the judgment. And the end of the 'times of the Gentiles' may simply be the end of history at Christ's return.
exchanges.answer: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that 'Blessed is he who comes' is a greeting of welcome from Psalms 118:26, not a cry of terror, so it fits a repentant Jerusalem better than a judged one. Zechariah 12:10 also pictures Jerusalem looking on the one they pierced and mourning in repentance. Three separate 'until' texts pointing the same way, they argue, form a pattern.

exchanges.title: Providence, survival, and the moral warning from Church history
exchanges.argument: Future-for-Israel writers point out that the Jewish people survived nearly two thousand years of exile, kept their identity, and returned in large numbers to the land, as many prophets foresaw (Isaiah 11:11-12; Ezekiel 36:24). They also warn that the claim that the church has replaced Israel has often been joined in history with contempt for Jews: for example, John Chrysostom's sermons against the Jews (386-387) and Luther's 'On the Jews and Their Lies' (1543). Soulen and Horner argue that supersessionism tends to see Jews as having no further purpose, and that this view made Christian hostility easier. Romans 11:18 warns Gentile branches not to boast against the natural branches.
exchanges.counter: Fulfilment writers grant the history and condemn it, but argue that a doctrine is judged by Scripture, not by misuse. Many fulfilment theologians have loved and protected Jewish people, and the view itself teaches that Jews are welcome in Christ on equal terms. They also note that Jewish survival and return can be acts of God's providence without being the fulfilment of covenant promises, since the Old Testament ties restoration to repentance (Deuteronomy 30:1-3), while the 1948 state was founded mostly by secular Zionists.
exchanges.answer: Future-for-Israel scholars reply that they do not claim the fulfilment view causes antisemitism, only that it removes a strong theological guard against it, which Romans 11:28-29 provides. On providence, they argue that God may regather Israel first in unbelief and then bring about repentance, as the order of Ezekiel 36:24-26 and Ezekiel 37:7-10 suggests: gathered, then cleansed; bones joined, then breath.

strawmen.strawman: 'Replacement theology' means God has rejected the Jews and Jews can no longer be saved.
strawmen.whyFalse: No major fulfilment theologian teaches that Jews cannot be saved. Paul, himself a Jew, says God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1-2) and that natural branches can be grafted in again (Romans 11:23). Many Reformed scholars, such as Murray, Vos and Hodge, even expect a future large-scale turning of Jews to Christ.
strawmen.accurate: The fulfilment view holds that Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ, the true Israel, and shared by all who trust him, Jew and Gentile alike. Most of its defenders reject the label 'replacement' and prefer 'fulfilment' or 'expansion': the believing remnant of Israel was never replaced, and Gentiles were added to Israel's one olive tree (Romans 11:17).

strawmen.strawman: Fulfilment theologians spiritualise everything, so they deny a physical resurrection and a real new earth.
strawmen.whyFalse: Covenant amillennialists, postmillennialists and progressive covenantalists confess the bodily resurrection and the bodily return of Christ, as the historic creeds do. Hoekema, Riddlebarger and Middleton argue strongly for a renewed, physical creation (Romans 8:19-23; Revelation 21:1-5).
strawmen.accurate: The fulfilment view reads Old Testament promises through their New Testament fulfilment in Christ. It holds that the land promise widens to the whole renewed earth (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5), which is a very physical hope. What it denies is a separate future ethnic inheritance of Canaan, not physical fulfilment as such.

strawmen.strawman: Fulfilment theology says God broke his promises to Israel.
strawmen.whyFalse: Fulfilment writers insist that God kept every promise, citing 2 Corinthians 1:20 and Joshua 21:43-45, which says not one of God's good promises to Israel failed. Their claim is that the promises were kept in a larger way than first expected, not that they were dropped.
strawmen.accurate: On this view God promised a Seed, a land, a throne and a temple, and he gave them in Christ: the Seed is Christ (Galatians 3:16), the throne is at God's right hand (Acts 2:30-36), the temple is Christ and his people (John 2:21; Ephesians 2:21), and the land becomes the world (Romans 4:13). Critics may judge this a reinterpretation, but its holders see it as faithful fulfilment.

strawmen.strawman: Anyone who holds the fulfilment view is antisemitic or anti-Jewish.
strawmen.whyFalse: A theological claim about how promises are fulfilled is not the same as hostility to a people. Many fulfilment theologians have opposed antisemitism; for example, members of the Confessing Church in Nazi Germany, many of them Reformed or Lutheran, resisted the persecution of Jews. Critics such as Soulen and Horner say supersessionism can make contempt easier, but they do not claim every holder is hostile.
strawmen.accurate: The fulfilment view holds that ethnic Jews are fully welcome in Christ, equal with Gentiles, and are not excluded from salvation. Its careful defenders accept the warning of Romans 11:18-20 against Gentile pride, and they condemn the anti-Jewish writings of Chrysostom and Luther as sin.

strawmen.whyFalse: Romans 11 is one of the most studied chapters among Reformed and amillennial scholars. There is a whole range of fulfilment readings: Calvin and Wright take 'all Israel' as the whole people of God; Robertson and Merkle take it as all elect Jews through history; Murray, Vos and Hodge expect a future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ.
strawmen.accurate: The fulfilment view takes Romans 11 seriously but reads its promise as salvation through faith in Christ under the new covenant (Romans 11:26-27), not as a restored national kingdom or temple. The disagreement is over what Romans 11 promises, not whether it matters.

strawmen.strawman: Dispensationalists teach two ways of salvation: by law for Israel, by grace for the church.
strawmen.whyFalse: Some early statements were unclear; a note in the 1909 Scofield Reference Bible on John 1:17 was widely read as contrasting legal obedience and grace as conditions of salvation. But dispensational leaders, including Ryrie and the editors of the New Scofield Reference Bible (1967), clearly reject salvation by works in any age.
strawmen.accurate: Dispensationalists hold that in every age salvation is by grace through faith, based on Christ's death. What changes from one dispensation to another is the content of revelation that faith responds to and the rule of life God gives, not the ground or means of salvation. Ryrie stated this as a central point in 'Dispensationalism'.

strawmen.strawman: Dispensationalists and Christian Zionists support anything the State of Israel does.
strawmen.whyFalse: Many dispensational scholars say that God's covenant with Israel does not mean approval of every policy of a modern secular government. Some, such as Vlach, separate the theological future of Israel from present political questions. Christian Zionist groups vary widely, and some also support Arab and Palestinian Christians.
strawmen.accurate: Most dispensationalists believe God has a future for ethnic Israel, and many see the 1948 state as at least a setting of the stage for that future. Christian Zionists go further and urge active support for the state, often citing Genesis 12:3. But support for the nation's existence is not the same as endorsing every act of its government, and many holders say so.

strawmen.strawman: Dispensationalism was invented out of nothing in 1830.
strawmen.whyFalse: Many of its parts are old. Premillennialism goes back to Justin Martyr and Irenaeus in the second century. Hope of a future Jewish conversion was common among Puritans (for example in Thomas Brightman, 1615, and later Increase Mather), and some English and Scottish writers expected a Jewish return to the land long before Darby.
strawmen.accurate: What is new in the 1830s, through John Nelson Darby and the Brethren, is the system: a sharp and lasting distinction between Israel and the church, a pre-tribulation rapture, and dividing history into dispensations in that particular way. It spread through the Niagara Bible Conferences and the Scofield Reference Bible (1909). Both the real roots and the real novelty should be stated.

strawmen.strawman: Dispensationalists think the church is an accident, a 'plan B' God did not intend.
strawmen.whyFalse: Classic dispensationalists, such as Chafer, Walvoord and Pentecost, called the church age a 'parenthesis' or 'intercalation', but they meant that it was not revealed in the Old Testament, not that God did not plan it. They point to Ephesians 3:5-6, which calls it a mystery hidden in past ages.
strawmen.accurate: Progressive dispensationalists, such as Blaising, Bock and Saucy, drop the 'parenthesis' language. They see the church as the present, inaugurated stage of the one kingdom plan, in which Christ already reigns from David's throne at God's right hand and Jews and Gentiles share the new covenant. Israel's national promises remain for the future stage.

strawmen.strawman: Dispensationalists believe Jews are saved by the Mosaic covenant without Jesus.
strawmen.whyFalse: Dual-covenant theology, which says Jews can be saved through their own covenant apart from Christ, is held by some liberal theologians and has been charged against a few popular figures. Mainstream dispensationalists strongly reject it. Arnold Fruchtenbaum, a leading dispensational writer, is a Messianic Jew who has spent his life preaching Jesus to Jewish people.
strawmen.accurate: Dispensationalists hold that there is salvation in no other name (Acts 4:12) for Jew or Gentile. They expect Israel's future national salvation to come when Israel looks on the one it pierced (Zechariah 12:10) and believes in Jesus as Messiah (Romans 11:26).

strawmen.strawman: Dispensationalists want war in the Middle East to hasten Armageddon.
strawmen.whyFalse: Scholarly dispensationalists teach that Christians cannot hasten or fix the date of prophetic events (Acts 1:7), and that believers should pray for peace and do good to all (1 Timothy 2:1-2; Galatians 6:10). Some popular prophecy writing has been sensational, and critics such as Weber and Gorenberg have documented its political influence, but that is not the same as wishing for war.
strawmen.accurate: Dispensationalists believe that a time of great tribulation and a final battle are foretold (Daniel 12:1; Zechariah 14:2-4), and that Christ will end it by his return. Expecting a foretold event is different from trying to cause it.

nodes.q: Does the New Testament have the final word on how Old Testament promises are fulfilled?
nodes.help: This is the main hermeneutical fork. If the New Testament can show a fuller meaning than the Old Testament text alone, promises may be fulfilled in Christ in a larger form; if not, the original sense must still be met.

options.label: Yes: the New Testament reveals how the promises are fulfilled, and may show a fuller meaning
No: the New Testament can add to an Old Testament promise but cannot change its original sense

nodes.q: Is Christ himself the true Israel and the one Seed, so that all who belong to him are heirs of Israel's promises?
nodes.help: Galatians 3:16 and 3:29 are central here. If Christ is the true Israel, Israel's identity runs through him to his people; the question is whether a separate national role remains.

options.label: Yes, and that settles who Israel is in the promises
Yes, but ethnic Israel still has a special future in God's plan

nodes.q: Are the land promises fulfilled, conditional, or still pending for ethnic Israel?
nodes.help: The land is the hardest test case. Joshua 21:43-45 says the promise was kept; Romans 4:13 widens it to the world; Amos 9:15 and Ezekiel 37:25 speak of a lasting possession.

options.label: Fulfilled in Joshua's day and now widened in Christ to the whole renewed earth
Conditional: lost through unfaithfulness, and now taken up into the greater promise in Christ
Still pending: the land belongs to ethnic Israel and will be fully possessed in the future

nodes.q: Does Romans 11:26 promise a future large-scale turning of ethnic Jews to Christ, and if so, what comes with it?
nodes.help: Even many Reformed scholars (Murray, Vos, Hodge) expect a future turning of Jews to Christ. The key question is whether a restored national kingdom in the land comes with it.

options.label: A large turning of Jews to Christ, but no restored national kingdom or temple
A turning to Christ that brings Israel's national restoration in the land under the Messiah

nodes.q: Does the thousand-year reign of Revelation 20 come after the second coming of Christ?
nodes.help: If Revelation 19 and 20 are in time order, a future earthly reign follows Christ's return. If Revelation 20 goes back to describe the present age, the millennium is now.

options.label: Yes: a future reign on earth follows Christ's return
No: Revelation 20 describes the present age between the two comings

nodes.q: How do you read the present age and the events of AD 70?
nodes.help: Fulfilment views agree that Christ reigns now. They differ over how much prophecy was fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem and how far the gospel will triumph before Christ returns.

options.label: AD 70 fulfilled most prophecies of judgment on Israel and ended the old covenant age
The gospel will win most of the nations before Christ returns
Good and evil grow together until Christ returns; the church suffers and witnesses

nodes.q: Is the founding of the State of Israel in 1948 a fulfilment of prophecy?
nodes.help: This separates the future-for-Israel camps. Some see 1948 as direct fulfilment that calls for support; others see a possible setting of the stage; others say the true restoration comes only with Israel's faith in Messiah.

options.label: Yes: it fulfils prophecy, and Christians should actively support the state (Genesis 12:3)
It may be a setting of the stage; Israel and the church remain distinct peoples with distinct promises
Not in itself a fulfilment; Israel's restoration comes with faith in Jesus, and Christ already reigns in part now

results.title: Covenant amillennialism
results.text: You read Israel's promises as fulfilled in Christ and shared by his one people, Jew and Gentile, with the millennium as the present reign of Christ. This is the view of Augustine, Calvin, Hoekema, Robertson and Riddlebarger. Progressive covenantalists such as Gentry and Wellum reach similar conclusions on Israel by a different account of the covenants.

results.title: Postmillennialism
results.text: You see Christ reigning now and expect the gospel to win most of the nations before he returns. Postmillennialists such as Mathison and Gentry read Israel's promises as fulfilled in Christ, though many, following the Puritans, expect a great conversion of Jews as part of that victory.

results.title: Partial preterism
results.text: You see AD 70 as the great judgment that ended the old covenant age and fulfilled much of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation. Partial preterists such as Gentry and DeMar hold that Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ and his church, while still expecting Christ's bodily return and final judgment.

results.title: Historic premillennialism
results.text: You expect a future earthly reign of Christ after his return, while seeing one people of God in Christ. Ladd and Blomberg represent this view; many of its holders expect a future turning of Jews to Christ (Romans 11:26) without a separate program for Israel.

results.title: Progressive dispensationalism
results.text: You see Christ already reigning on David's throne and the church as the present stage of the one kingdom plan, while Israel's national promises await fulfilment when Israel turns to Jesus. Blaising, Bock and Saucy represent this view.

results.title: Classic dispensationalism
results.text: You hold that Israel and the church are distinct peoples with distinct promises, and that Israel's national kingdom will come in a future millennium after Christ's return. Darby, Scofield, Walvoord, Ryrie and Pentecost are leading names; many see 1948 as a setting of the stage.

results.title: Christian Zionism
results.text: You see the 1948 state as a fulfilment of prophecy and believe Christians should actively support it, often citing Genesis 12:3. Christian Zionism has roots in 19th century British restorationism and today is strong among many evangelical groups; its holders vary on politics.

quiz.q: In Acts 15:16-17, which Old Testament passage does James quote about rebuilding David's fallen tent?
quiz.explain: James quotes Amos 9:11-12 to show that Gentiles coming to faith fits the prophets. Fulfilment writers see the rebuilding of David's tent in the church; dispensationalists often see the Gentile mission as a step before Israel's future restoration.

quiz.q: In which year was the Balfour Declaration issued?
quiz.explain: Arthur Balfour, the British Foreign Secretary, signed the declaration on 2 November 1917. It supported 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine, while saying the rights of existing non-Jewish communities must not be harmed.

quiz.q: What does Paul stress in Galatians 3:16?
options: That the law came 430 years after the promise
That the promise was spoken to one 'seed', singular, which is Christ
That Abraham was justified before he was circumcised
That the land is an everlasting possession
quiz.explain: Paul notes that the promise speaks of 'seed', not 'seeds', and names that one Seed as Christ. Galatians 3:29 then says all who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed.

quiz.q: Which chapter of Ezekiel contains the vision of the valley of dry bones?
quiz.explain: Ezekiel 37:1-14 shows dry bones coming together and then receiving breath, a picture of Israel restored from exile. Some read it of 1948; others read it of spiritual resurrection by the Spirit.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'Der Judenstaat' (The Jewish State) in 1896?
quiz.explain: Theodor Herzl, an Austro-Hungarian journalist, wrote it in 1896 and organised the First Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897. His Zionism was largely secular and political in aim.

quiz.q: On what date did the United Nations General Assembly vote for the partition of Palestine (Resolution 181)?
quiz.explain: Resolution 181 was adopted on 29 November 1947. The State of Israel declared its independence on 14 May 1948.

quiz.q: Which passage tells of a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passing between the halves of the animals?
quiz.explain: In Genesis 15:17 only God's presence passes between the pieces. Dispensationalists see this as proof that the land covenant is unconditional; fulfilment writers agree it rests on God and say he keeps it in Christ.

quiz.q: Which Old Testament text gives Israel the titles 'kingdom of priests' and 'holy nation' that 1 Peter 2:9 applies to believers?
quiz.explain: Exodus 19:5-6 records these titles at Sinai. Peter gives them to the church, which the fulfilment camp reads as a transfer of Israel's identity to the people of Christ.

quiz.q: Who is usually named as the main early systematiser of dispensationalism in the 1830s?
quiz.explain: John Nelson Darby of the Plymouth Brethren shaped the system in the 1830s. Scofield spread it widely through his Reference Bible (1909); Chafer and Ryrie developed it later.

quiz.q: Which verse says the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable, in the context of Israel?
quiz.explain: Romans 11:28-29 says Israel is beloved for the fathers' sake, because God's gifts and calling cannot be revoked. Future-for-Israel scholars rely on this heavily; fulfilment scholars read it of Israel's salvation in Christ.

quiz.q: Which New Testament book calls the first covenant 'obsolete' and 'ready to vanish away' after quoting Jeremiah 31?
quiz.explain: Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes the new covenant from Jeremiah 31:31-34, and Hebrews 8:13 draws the conclusion. Fulfilment writers use this against a future return to temple sacrifices.

quiz.q: In what year did the Roman army under Titus destroy the Jerusalem temple?
quiz.explain: The temple was burned in AD 70 after a long siege, as Josephus records in 'The Jewish War'. The war began in AD 66; the Bar Kokhba revolt was crushed in AD 135.

bestCase.fulfilment: The fulfilment case begins with the apostles' own words: every promise of God has found its 'Yes' in Jesus (2 Corinthians 1:20), and the promise to Abraham was made to his seed, 'who is Christ' (Galatians 3:16). Jesus relives Israel's story, from Egypt to the wilderness to the mountain, and succeeds where the nation failed, so that he is the true Israel, the true vine and the true temple (Matthew 2:15; John 15:1; John 2:21). The New Testament then applies Israel's titles, covenant and hope to all who are in him: believing Gentiles are Abraham's seed (Galatians 3:29), a royal priesthood and holy nation (1 Peter 2:9), and members of the commonwealth of Israel (Ephesians 2:12, 19). Abraham himself looked beyond Canaan to a heavenly country, and Paul says he was promised the world (Hebrews 11:16; Romans 4:13), which is why the meek inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). Peter preached that the risen Christ already sits on David's throne (Acts 2:30-36), and James saw David's fallen tent rebuilt as Gentiles turned to God (Acts 15:16-17). Hebrews calls the old order a shadow now obsolete (Hebrews 8:13), so a return to an earthly temple and land program would be a step backwards. On this reading nothing God promised has failed; it has all been kept, and kept more gloriously than Israel first imagined, in Christ and his one people.
bestCase.future: The future case begins with the character of God: he swore by himself to Abraham (Hebrews 6:13), cut the covenant alone (Genesis 15:17-18), and tied Israel's survival as a nation to the fixed order of the sun and moon (Jeremiah 31:35-37). Promises given to a specific people about a specific land, with specific borders, cannot be fully kept by giving something else to someone else, however glorious. Paul, writing after the cross, still says that to his unbelieving kinsmen belong 'the covenants' and 'the promises' (Romans 9:4), that they are beloved for the fathers' sake, and that God's calling of them is irrevocable (Romans 11:28-29). The apostles asked the risen Jesus when, not whether, he would restore the kingdom to Israel, and he corrected only their timing (Acts 1:6-7); Peter later spoke of a coming 'restoration of all things' spoken by the prophets (Acts 3:21). Jesus promised the twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes 'in the regeneration' (Matthew 19:28) and told Jerusalem it would see him again when it welcomed him (Matthew 23:39). The New Testament adds Gentiles to Israel's blessings, as the prophets foretold (Isaiah 19:24-25), without cancelling Israel's own inheritance. On this reading, God's faithfulness to Israel is the guarantee of his faithfulness to the church.
